purpose: Presentation-only teaching layer for the Hays Botany visual learner. Canonical taxonomy/range/morphology remains in content/taxa.

simple.label: Simple
simple.description: Recognize the plant using a few high-value field cues.

terms.label: Learn Terms
terms.description: Learn the botanical vocabulary while looking at the structure it names.
terms.mantra: See it → name it → use it.

field.label: Field Botany
field.description: Use technical morphology, family structure, range evidence, and comparisons.

Asteraceae.plain_signature: What looks like one flower is usually a whole flower head made of many tiny florets.
Asteraceae.look_here_first: Turn the flower head sideways. Inspect the green bracts underneath—the phyllaries—and notice whether the head has ray florets, disc florets, or both.
Asteraceae.field_signature: A capitulum of many florets on a receptacle, subtended by an involucre of phyllaries; fruit is a cypsela, often with a pappus.
Asteraceae.field_question: Before looking at flower color, what do the phyllaries and floret types look like?
Asteraceae.caveat: Asteraceae is extremely diverse. Not every member has showy ray florets.

Apocynaceae.plain_signature: Broad dogbanes share a fused-flower plan; our local milkweed group adds the corona, gynostegium and pollinia machinery.
Apocynaceae.look_here_first: Broad family: check latex, simple usually opposite/whorled leaves and a fused 5-lobed corolla. In milkweeds/milkvines, go straight to corona + gynostegium.
Apocynaceae.field_signature: Broad family commonly has a fused corolla, five stamens and a superior two-carpel gynoecium. Derived Asclepiadoideae adds a corona, gynostegium, pollinia/pollinarium and commonly follicle fruit with comose seeds.
Apocynaceae.field_question: Am I seeing the broad dogbane plan, or the more specialized milkweed reproductive machinery?
Apocynaceae.caveat: Corona, gynostegium and pollinia are excellent milkweed-side characters, not mandatory across all Apocynaceae.

Convolvulaceae.plain_signature: Five persistent sepals sit behind a fused pleated corolla; alternate leaves and a capsule complete the common local pattern.
Convolvulaceae.look_here_first: Look behind the flower first: five usually free persistent sepals, then the folds of the fused funnel/bell corolla.
Convolvulaceae.field_signature: Typically alternate exstipulate leaves; 5 free/persistent sepals; sympetalous plicate corolla; superior ovary; commonly a dry capsule.
Convolvulaceae.field_question: What do the sepals and corolla folds look like—and does the fruit become a capsule?
Convolvulaceae.caveat: Heart-shaped leaves and twining habit are common, not mandatory. Dodders are extreme parasitic exceptions.

Fagaceae.plain_signature: For our local oaks, the acorn and its cupule prove the family; mature leaves, buds, twigs and bark separate the species.
Fagaceae.look_here_first: If fruit is present, start with the acorn and scaly cupule. Then read a mature leaf and the twig/bud.
Fagaceae.field_signature: Woody plants with alternate simple leaves and a nut associated with a cupule; in Quercus this is the acorn.
Fagaceae.field_question: Do I have a true acorn/cupule, and what do the mature leaf and buds say?
Fagaceae.caveat: Catkins alone are not enough—walnuts have catkins too. Oak leaves also vary on one tree.

Papaveraceae.plain_signature: Quickly falling sepals, many free stamens and a capsule matter more than petal color in our prickly poppies.
Papaveraceae.look_here_first: For Argemone, inspect the bud/sepals and then the capsule prickles. Use latex only as supporting evidence and avoid unnecessary damage.
Papaveraceae.field_signature: Common pattern: caducous 2–3 sepals, free petals, numerous free stamens, superior syncarpous ovary and many-seeded capsule.
Papaveraceae.field_question: Are the stamens free, and what is the capsule-prickle architecture?
Papaveraceae.caveat: The current learner is Argemone-heavy, so prickles and latex are especially useful locally rather than universal family rules.

Poaceae.plain_signature: Jointed stems and a leaf sheath/collar/ligule lead you to the spikelet—the tiny unit that actually carries the grass flowers.
Poaceae.look_here_first: Start at a node, then pull the leaf blade away from the culm and inspect the sheath, collar and ligule. If flowering, isolate one spikelet.
Poaceae.field_signature: Usually jointed culms with obvious nodes; leaves with sheath + blade + ligule; reduced flowers arranged as florets inside spikelets with glumes, lemma and palea.
Poaceae.field_question: Is there a real node, and what does the collar/ligule look like before I even touch the flower head?
Poaceae.caveat: Grass color and general fuzziness are weak ID characters. Use architecture and spikelet parts.

Fabaceae.plain_signature: The flowers and leaves can look wildly different, but one superior carpel becoming a legume ties the family together.
Fabaceae.look_here_first: Look for a pod or developing ovary first. Then check stipules, pulvini and leaf architecture before judging the flower shape.
Fabaceae.field_signature: Usually alternate stipulate leaves, often with pulvini; one superior carpel/locule; fruit usually a legume or modified legume. Flowers may be papilionoid, caesalpinioid-like or mimosoid.
Fabaceae.field_question: What does the single carpel become—and are stipules or pulvini supporting the ID?
Fabaceae.caveat: Do not require a classic pea flower or pinnately compound leaves.

Lamiaceae.plain_signature: Opposite leaves get your attention; a deeply 4-lobed ovary and the fruit pattern do the real confirming.
Lamiaceae.look_here_first: Start at the node for opposite/decussate leaves and no stipules. Then inspect the tubular flower, ovary/style and persistent calyx.
Lamiaceae.field_signature: Common pattern: opposite exstipulate leaves, often quadrangular aromatic stem, tubular/bilabiate flower, 2 or 4 stamens, superior often 4-lobed ovary and usually four nutlets.
Lamiaceae.field_question: After I notice opposite leaves, does the flower center resolve into the mint-family ovary/style/fruit pattern?
Lamiaceae.caveat: Square stems, aroma, bilabiate flowers and four nutlets are common—not universal. Salvia has two fertile stamens; Callicarpa is drupaceous.

Malvaceae.plain_signature: In our local mallow lesson, many stamens fuse into a conspicuous column around the style.
Malvaceae.look_here_first: Go straight to the flower center for the staminal column, then check stipules, palmate venation/stellate hairs and the fruit.
Malvaceae.field_signature: Local Malvoideae commonly has alternate stipulate leaves, stellate hairs, 5-part flowers, a staminal column, superior ovary and segmented fruit.
Malvaceae.field_question: Are the many stamens free—or fused into a column around the style?
Malvaceae.caveat: The staminal-column pattern is excellent for our local Malvoideae anchors, but broad Malvaceae is more diverse.

Asparagaceae.plain_signature: For local Yucca, read the true fibrous leaf rosette first, then confirm the six-part flower and fruit.
Asparagaceae.look_here_first: Compare rosette/trunk architecture, leaf width/rigidity, margin fibers and terminal spine; then inspect the terminal flower panicle.
Asparagaceae.field_signature: Our Yucca anchors have true fibrous leaves, 3+3 tepals, 6 stamens and a 3-carpellate fruit; broad modern Asparagaceae is much more diverse.
Asparagaceae.field_question: What do the leaf architecture and armature say before I use the flower?
Asparagaceae.caveat: Do not treat the Yucca rosette as a universal Asparagaceae character.

Ranunculaceae.plain_signature: Many free stamens and mostly free carpels are the core; in Clematis the showy parts are sepals, not petals.
Ranunculaceae.look_here_first: Go to the flower center for numerous free stamens and carpels, then ask whether the showy structures are sepals or petals.
Ranunculaceae.field_signature: Common pattern: superior ovary, many free stamens, one to many mostly free carpels, free sepals often petaloid, and aggregate achenes or follicles.
Ranunculaceae.field_question: Are the reproductive parts free, and am I accidentally calling petaloid sepals 'petals'?
Ranunculaceae.caveat: The current visual module is Clematis-heavy; other Ranunculaceae can look very different.

Anacardiaceae.plain_signature: Woody alternate leaves plus one-seeded drupes get you close; leaflet number, rachis form and fruit finish the job.
Anacardiaceae.look_here_first: Read the leaf architecture first—trifoliolate or odd-pinnate, winged rachis or not—then confirm with the drupe cluster.
Anacardiaceae.field_signature: Local pattern: woody, alternate exstipulate leaves, resinous tissues, small flowers with a nectar disk, superior ovary and one-seeded drupes.
Anacardiaceae.field_question: After I count the leaflets, what does the rachis and fruit cluster say?
Anacardiaceae.caveat: Never use sap contact as an ID test; poison-ivy relatives can cause dermatitis.

Cupressaceae.plain_signature: Tiny scale leaves and cones—not flowers or true fruits—define the local juniper lesson.
Cupressaceae.look_here_first: Inspect the foliage and cone type. Ashe juniper has scale leaves and fleshy blue female seed cones.
Cupressaceae.field_signature: Conifers with scale/awl/linear leaves and seed cones whose scale/bract units are fused; local Juniperus has fleshy seed cones.
Cupressaceae.field_question: Am I looking at a true fruit—or a modified seed cone?
Cupressaceae.caveat: Cupressaceae is not always evergreen or scale-leaved; Taxodium is the major local exception.

Onagraceae.plain_signature: Look under the petals: the flower sits above an inferior ovary, often on a floral tube, with a repeated four-part plan.
Onagraceae.look_here_first: Find the green ovary below the petals and trace the floral tube upward; then check the 4-lobed stigma.
Onagraceae.field_signature: Local Oenothera commonly has an inferior ovary, hypanthium/floral tube, 4 sepals, 4 petals, 4 or 8 stamens and a 4-lobed stigma.
Onagraceae.field_question: Where is the ovary relative to the petals, and is this a classic primrose or former-Gaura form?
Onagraceae.caveat: Flower color, symmetry, stamen count and fruit type all vary within the local set.

Ebenaceae.plain_signature: Alternate entire leaves plus a fleshy berry sitting on a persistent calyx make the local persimmon pattern.
Ebenaceae.look_here_first: For Texas persimmon, read bark first, then the small entire leaves and the berry with retained calyx lobes.
Ebenaceae.field_signature: Woody plants with alternate exstipulate leaves, fused small flowers, superior multi-loculed ovary and fleshy berries with a persistent often enlarged calyx.
Ebenaceae.field_question: Does the developing fruit keep a conspicuous calyx beneath it?
Ebenaceae.caveat: Do not use fruit color alone; bark, leaf size/pubescence and flower anatomy matter.

Oleaceae.plain_signature: Opposite woody branching gets your attention; ash samaras versus Forestiera drupes finish the local family lesson.
Oleaceae.look_here_first: Start at the node for opposite/subopposite leaves with no stipules, then ask whether the plant has compound ash leaves or simple Forestiera leaves.
Oleaceae.field_signature: Local Oleaceae is woody and exstipulate; Fraxinus has odd-pinnate leaves + samaras, Forestiera simple leaves + drupes.
Oleaceae.field_question: What does the fruit become—single-winged samara or one-seeded drupe?
Oleaceae.caveat: Do not reduce Oleaceae to opposite leaves or four white petals; local focal genera often have tiny or apetalous flowers.

Rosaceae.plain_signature: Stipules plus a hypanthium set up the flower; fruit architecture tells you which Rosaceae branch you are looking at.
Rosaceae.look_here_first: Check for stipules, then a hypanthium and many stamens; next identify the fruit type.
Rosaceae.field_signature: Usually alternate stipulate leaves, radial flowers with a hypanthium and often many stamens; fruit may be drupe, pome, aggregate drupelets or aggregate achenes.
Rosaceae.field_question: After I recognize the Rosaceae flower plan, what kind of fruit does it build?
Rosaceae.caveat: Five petals + many stamens is not enough by itself. Fruit architecture is essential.

Sapindaceae.plain_signature: Maple, soapberry and Mexican buckeye look unrelated, so use the reproductive plan and fruit diversity instead of one leaf rule.
Sapindaceae.look_here_first: Start with fruit and leaf arrangement: paired samara, translucent drupe-like fruit, or 3-valved capsule.
Sapindaceae.field_signature: Woody plants, usually exstipulate, often with a floral disk and superior 2–3-carpellate ovary; local fruits range from samaras to drupes to capsules.
Sapindaceae.field_question: What fruit architecture am I looking at, and is the leaf arrangement opposite or alternate?
Sapindaceae.caveat: No single leaf arrangement or fruit type defines Sapindaceae.

Aquifoliaceae.plain_signature: Alternate simple leaves plus tiny unisexual flowers lead to a small drupe with several hard pyrenes.
Aquifoliaceae.look_here_first: Compare deciduous versus evergreen habit and leaf texture, then inspect tiny axillary flowers and fruit.
Aquifoliaceae.field_signature: Woody Ilex with alternate simple leaves, tiny mostly 4–5-merous unisexual flowers, superior ovary and multi-pyrene drupe.
Aquifoliaceae.field_question: Is this possumhaw, yaupon, or a lookalike—and what do the leaf texture and pyrene-bearing fruit say?
Aquifoliaceae.caveat: Red fruit is not enough; local hollies differ strongly in habit and leaf texture.

Ulmaceae.plain_signature: Trace the leaf veins: many pinnate side veins running into serrations plus a dry samara strongly favors elm.
Ulmaceae.look_here_first: Hold the leaf flat and follow the secondary veins from the midrib to the margin, then look for a samara.
Ulmaceae.field_signature: Alternate simple often asymmetric leaves with pinnate venation and serrate margins; Ulmus fruit is a one-winged samara.
Ulmaceae.field_question: Do I have elm-style pinnate venation and a samara, or hackberry-style basal veins and a drupe?
Ulmaceae.caveat: Hackberries are Cannabaceae in modern classification but are the most useful local elm comparison.

Verbenaceae.plain_signature: Opposite leaves and spikes/heads get you close; style position and fruit architecture separate the family from the mints.
Verbenaceae.look_here_first: Start with opposite exstipulate leaves and a racemose spike/head, then inspect ovary/style and fruit.
Verbenaceae.field_signature: Usually opposite leaves, racemose/spicate/capitate inflorescences, tubular zygomorphic flowers, superior ovary and commonly terminal style.
Verbenaceae.field_question: Is the inflorescence racemose, and is the style terminal rather than gynobasic?
Verbenaceae.caveat: Square stems and aroma do not separate Verbenaceae from Lamiaceae.

Bignoniaceae.plain_signature: Woody opposite-leaved plants with showy trumpet flowers become convincing Bignoniaceae when the long capsule opens to flat winged seeds.
Bignoniaceae.look_here_first: Check woody habit and opposite leaves, then find the long capsule and flattened winged seeds.
Bignoniaceae.field_signature: Woody vines/trees/shrubs, opposite often compound leaves, tubular zygomorphic flowers, usually 4 didynamous stamens + staminode, superior ovary, 2-valved capsule with winged seeds.
Bignoniaceae.field_question: Does the woody plant end in a long capsule full of flat winged seeds?
Bignoniaceae.caveat: Trumpet-shaped flowers alone are not enough; fruit and woody architecture matter.

Plantaginaceae.plain_signature: For Penstemon, look inside the bilateral tube for four fertile stamens plus the sterile beardtongue, then confirm a many-seeded capsule.
Plantaginaceae.look_here_first: Inspect the flower interior for the staminode, then the fruit.
Plantaginaceae.field_signature: Mostly herbs with fused often zygomorphic corollas, commonly 2 or 4 fertile stamens, superior ovary and many-seeded capsule.
Plantaginaceae.field_question: Is there a sterile fifth stamen—and does the fruit become a capsule rather than nutlets?
Plantaginaceae.caveat: The beardtongue is a Penstemon hook, not a universal Plantaginaceae character.

Apiaceae.plain_signature: Do not demand an umbrella. Inferior ovary + stylopodium + a fruit splitting into two mericarps is the safer family pattern.
Apiaceae.look_here_first: Start at the inflorescence, then verify ovary position and the two-part schizocarp.
Apiaceae.field_signature: Mostly herbs with sheathing leaf bases, 5-merous flowers, inferior 2-carpellate ovary, two styles often on a stylopodium, and a dry schizocarp splitting into 2 mericarps.
Apiaceae.field_question: Where is the ovary, and does the mature fruit split into two one-seeded halves?
Apiaceae.caveat: Eryngium shows why 'white umbrella flowers' is not a family definition.

Rubiaceae.plain_signature: The node gives it away: opposite/whorled leaves with interpetiolar stipules, then an inferior ovary.
Rubiaceae.look_here_first: Look between opposite petiole bases for the stipules before studying the flower.
Rubiaceae.field_signature: Simple opposite/whorled leaves + interpetiolar stipules + fused mostly radial flower + stamens matching corolla lobes + inferior ovary.
Rubiaceae.field_question: Are there stipules sitting between the opposite leaf bases?
Rubiaceae.caveat: Opposite leaves alone are weak; several unrelated families share them.

Sapotaceae.plain_signature: Sticky/milky latex plus alternate entire leaves leads to tiny axillary flowers and a fleshy fruit with a hard glossy seed.
Sapotaceae.look_here_first: Use woody habit, alternate entire leaves and naturally exposed latex first, then inspect tiny axillary flower clusters.
Sapotaceae.field_signature: Woody plants with latex, alternate entire leaves, fused radial flowers, superior ovary, berry-like fruit and hard shiny seeds.
Sapotaceae.field_question: Do I have latex plus tiny axillary flowers and a hard glossy seed?
Sapotaceae.caveat: Do not injure plants solely to test latex.

Commelinaceae.plain_signature: Soft jointed stems and sheathing parallel-veined leaves lead to a 3-sepal + 3-petal flower plan.
Commelinaceae.look_here_first: Start at the node and leaf sheath, then count the flower parts.
Commelinaceae.field_signature: Jointed somewhat succulent herbs, alternate parallel-veined sheathing leaves, 3 sepals + 3 petals, variable fertile stamens/staminodes, superior 3-carpellate ovary and capsule.
Commelinaceae.field_question: Is the leaf base sheathing a soft jointed stem, and does the flower use a 3+3 plan?
Commelinaceae.caveat: Do not teach every member as three equal blue petals; Commelina is strongly asymmetric.

Berberidaceae.plain_signature: Local barberries pair yellow inner tissue and spiny leathery leaflets with a layered yellow flower and berry fruit.
Berberidaceae.look_here_first: Start with the evergreen spiny shrub and yellow inner tissue, then inspect the flower's multiple perianth whorls and anther mechanism.
Berberidaceae.field_signature: Local Berberis has alternate compound leaves, multiple petaloid sepal whorls, 6 nectar-bearing petals, 6 stamens opposite the petals, a superior ovary, and berry fruit.
Berberidaceae.field_question: Does the flower have layered petaloid sepals plus six petals and valve-opening anthers?
Berberidaceae.caveat: Valve-opening anthers are excellent for Berberis, not a universal Berberidaceae rule.

Orobanchaceae.plain_signature: Many local members are green root hemiparasites with bracted spikes, tubular flowers, and many-seeded capsules.
Orobanchaceae.look_here_first: Look at the bracted inflorescence and fused bilateral corolla, but remember the parasitic connection is underground.
Orobanchaceae.field_signature: Green or non-green root parasites with simple exstipulate leaves when present, tubular zygomorphic flowers, usually 4 stamens, superior ovary, and a many-seeded capsule.
Orobanchaceae.field_question: Is this a green hemiparasite with a bracted spike and capsule rather than a mint-style nutlet fruit?
Orobanchaceae.caveat: Do not uproot plants to verify haustoria, and do not assume all parasitic plants are pale or leafless.

Passifloraceae.plain_signature: Axillary tendrils plus a corona and elevated reproductive column make passionflowers hard to confuse once you know the parts.
Passifloraceae.look_here_first: At a node, check whether the tendril is axillary; then inspect the flower corona and raised stamens/ovary.
Passifloraceae.field_signature: Alternate stipulate leaves, axillary tendrils, 5 sepals + 5 petals, conspicuous corona, androgynophore/gynophore, superior ovary, and berry-like/capsular fruit.
Passifloraceae.field_question: Is the tendril in the leaf axil, and does the flower have a corona plus elevated reproductive column?
Passifloraceae.caveat: Leaf lobing alone is weak; tendril position is a much better vine-family character.

Vitaceae.plain_signature: On a grape vine, check what sits opposite the leaf: a tendril or inflorescence there is a major clue.
Vitaceae.look_here_first: At the node, find the structure opposite the leaf, then confirm tiny flowers and berry fruit.
Vitaceae.field_signature: Woody climbers with alternate stipulate leaves, commonly leaf-opposed tendrils/inflorescences, tiny actinomorphic flowers, superior ovary, and berry fruit.
Vitaceae.field_question: Is the tendril opposite the leaf rather than sitting in its axil?
Vitaceae.caveat: Do not identify grape family from a lobed leaf alone.

Cannabaceae.plain_signature: For local hackberries, three strong veins from the leaf base plus a fleshy drupe are the fast combination.
Cannabaceae.look_here_first: Trace the major veins from the petiole, then check whether the fruit is fleshy rather than winged.
Cannabaceae.field_signature: Local Celtis has alternate simple often asymmetric leaves, strong basal 3-vein architecture, and a thinly fleshy drupe with a hard stone.
Cannabaceae.field_question: Do three strong veins rise from the leaf base, and does the plant make a drupe rather than a samara?
Cannabaceae.caveat: Modern classification places Celtis in Cannabaceae rather than Ulmaceae.

Acanthaceae.plain_signature: Tubular flowers get you close; the capsule and its hook-like seed supports are the stronger family characters.
Acanthaceae.look_here_first: If fruit is present, inspect the capsule interior for retinacula supporting the seeds.
Acanthaceae.field_signature: Usually opposite simple leaves, tubular zygomorphic flowers, 2 or 4 stamens, superior 2-locular ovary, and loculicidal capsule with retinacula in many local forms.
Acanthaceae.field_question: Does the capsule contain the characteristic seed-support hooks?
Acanthaceae.caveat: Flower shape alone overlaps strongly with other Lamiales families.

Aristolochiaceae.plain_signature: The bizarre flower is the shortcut: one fused petaloid perianth tube, no ordinary petal corolla, and an inferior ovary.
Aristolochiaceae.look_here_first: Ignore the leaf shape at first and inspect the flower tube and its position above the ovary.
Aristolochiaceae.field_signature: Alternate exstipulate leaves, strongly specialized fused perianth/calyx, petals absent in Aristolochia, inferior ovary, gynostemium, and many-seeded capsule.
Aristolochiaceae.field_question: Am I looking at a true corolla—or a petaloid fused calyx/perianth sitting above an inferior ovary?
Aristolochiaceae.caveat: Local A. erecta is small and erect/sprawling, not a giant tropical pipevine.

Cactaceae.plain_signature: Find the areole first. Pads, spines, glochids, flowers, and branches all make more sense after that.
Cactaceae.look_here_first: Locate a true areole, then ask what it produces and how the stem is segmented.
Cactaceae.field_signature: Succulent stems with specialized areoles; leaves often reduced; flowers commonly many-parted with many stamens; inferior ovary; fleshy many-seeded fruit.
Cactaceae.field_question: Can I identify a true areole rather than just a thorny succulent stem?
Cactaceae.caveat: Flattened pads and glochids are Opuntia-side characters, not universal across Cactaceae.

Ericaceae.plain_signature: Fused urn/bell-shaped flowers get you close; poricidal anthers are the high-value technical confirmation.
Ericaceae.look_here_first: Inspect the fused corolla, then zoom to how the anthers release pollen.
Ericaceae.field_signature: Woody or herbaceous plants, usually exstipulate, commonly sympetalous, with 5–10 stamens often bearing poricidal anthers; ovary position and fruit type vary.
Ericaceae.field_question: Do the anthers release pollen through small terminal pores?
Ericaceae.caveat: Do not memorize one ovary position or one fruit type for Ericaceae.

Juglandaceae.plain_signature: Alternate pinnately compound leaves plus a husked nut are the local walnut-family combination.
Juglandaceae.look_here_first: Start with the long compound leaf, then find catkins and the husked nut.
Juglandaceae.field_signature: Woody trees with alternate pinnately compound exstipulate leaves, unisexual flowers, male catkins, and a one-seeded nut enclosed by an outer husk.
Juglandaceae.field_question: Is this a compound-leaved tree with a husked nut rather than an acorn in a cupule?
Juglandaceae.caveat: Catkins alone do not separate walnuts from oaks.

Platanaceae.plain_signature: Mottled bark and giant lobed leaves are obvious, but the hidden axillary bud and many-achene fruiting ball are better structural lessons.
Platanaceae.look_here_first: Check that the leaves are alternate, then inspect the swollen petiole base, ring-like stipule scar, and spherical fruiting heads.
Platanaceae.field_signature: Large deciduous trees with alternate palmately lobed leaves, petiole base enclosing the axillary bud, annular stipule scar, unisexual spherical flower heads, and spherical aggregates of achenes.
Platanaceae.field_question: Is that hanging ball one fruit—or a head made of many separate achenes?
Platanaceae.caveat: Mottled bark is supporting evidence; younger trunks may not show the classic patchwork strongly.

Pteridaceae.plain_signature: Flip the frond over: marginal sori and a rolled blade edge acting as a false indusium are the key local cliffbrake lesson.
Pteridaceae.look_here_first: Read the frond divisions, then inspect the underside and margins for sori.
Pteridaceae.field_signature: Ferns with spores rather than seeds; many local cheilanthoids have marginal/submarginal sori and a recurved blade margin forming a false indusium.
Pteridaceae.field_question: Where are the sori, and is their covering a separate indusium or simply the rolled blade margin?
Pteridaceae.caveat: False indusia are common in the local cliffbrake framework but not universal across all Pteridaceae.

Alismataceae.plain_signature: Aquatic rosettes can change leaf form dramatically; the flower stalk and many-achene fruit head tie the forms together.
Alismataceae.look_here_first: Compare submerged and emergent leaves, then read the flower stalk from bottom to top.
Alismataceae.field_signature: Local Sagittaria anchor: aquatic heterophylly, 3-part flowers, pistillate flowers below staminate flowers, and a spherical head of many achenes.
Alismataceae.field_question: Are the underwater and above-water leaves really the same species—and what does the inflorescence prove?
Alismataceae.caveat: Do not require arrow-shaped leaves; Sagittaria platyphylla often lacks deep sagittate lobes.

Cabombaceae.plain_signature: Opposite underwater leaves split into fine fan-shaped segments, then a tiny 3-part flower reaches the surface.
Cabombaceae.look_here_first: Ignore the flower first: check whether the submerged leaves are opposite and fan-shaped.
Cabombaceae.field_signature: Rooted submerged aquatic with opposite finely divided leaves and small 3-merous surface flowers in the local Cabomba anchor.
Cabombaceae.field_question: Are the feathery leaves opposite fans or arranged some other way?
Cabombaceae.caveat: This local lesson is Cabomba-centered; broad Cabombaceae contains more variation.

Pontederiaceae.plain_signature: A grasslike aquatic plant can reveal its real identity when a showy 6-part flower appears.
Pontederiaceae.look_here_first: On Heteranthera dubia, pair the linear aquatic leaves with the solitary yellow flower.
Pontederiaceae.field_signature: Local Heteranthera anchor: aquatic monocot, 6-part perianth, 3 stamens, capsule, and mirror-image floral handedness.
Pontederiaceae.field_question: What happens when I stop judging the plant by its grasslike leaves and inspect the flower?
Pontederiaceae.caveat: Linear leaves and yellow flowers are Heteranthera traits, not universal Pontederiaceae characters.

Potamogetonaceae.plain_signature: The key clue is often hiding at the leaf axil: a pondweed stipule plus two-ranked submerged leaves and an emergent flower spike.
Potamogetonaceae.look_here_first: Inspect the leaf axil underwater for the persistent stipule/prophyll before using leaf width.
Potamogetonaceae.field_signature: Local Potamogeton anchor: alternate distichous leaves, conspicuous axillary stipule/prophyll, emergent dense flower spike, and small one-seeded fruits.
Potamogetonaceae.field_question: Can I find the axillary stipule, and does the stem lead to a true pondweed spike?
Potamogetonaceae.caveat: Leaf width alone is unreliable for broad-leaved Potamogeton identification.

Euphorbiaceae.plain_signature: Many spurges reduce their flowers dramatically; a superior 3-part ovary/capsule is often more useful than the flower outline.
Euphorbiaceae.look_here_first: Check for latex without damaging the plant, then inspect whether the flowers are unisexual/reduced and whether the fruit follows a three-part capsule plan.
Euphorbiaceae.field_signature: Common pattern: alternate simple leaves, often latex, reduced unisexual flowers, superior usually 3-locular ovary, and a 3-part capsule/schizocarp.
Euphorbiaceae.field_question: Are these reduced male/female flowers leading to a three-part fruit rather than a normal showy bisexual flower?
Euphorbiaceae.caveat: Cyathia are characteristic of Euphorbia, not a requirement for all Euphorbiaceae.

asclepias-tuberosa.standout: A major milkweed exception in this set: the sap is clear/watery rather than milky.
asclepias-tuberosa.family_connection: It still has the specialized milkweed flower architecture—corona, hoods, and gynostegium.

asclepias-verticillata.standout: The needle-thin leaves are arranged in obvious whorls around the stem.
asclepias-verticillata.family_connection: Leaf phyllotaxy narrows the milkweeds quickly before you even inspect the flower.

asclepias-viridis.standout: The broad leaves plus green flowers and hood structure make this milkweed distinctive.
asclepias-viridis.family_connection: The corona and gynostegium are still the high-value milkweed structures.

helianthus-maximiliani.standout: Look for the tall perennial colony with many narrow, often drooping leaves.
helianthus-maximiliani.family_connection: Then confirm Asteraceae structure at the head: phyllaries outside, florets packed on the receptacle.

helianthus-annuus.standout: Usually broader leaves and more branching than Maximilian sunflower.
helianthus-annuus.family_connection: Use the involucre and phyllaries to move beyond the generic 'yellow sunflower' impression.

argemone-albiflora-subsp-texana.standout: Do not rely on white petals alone—latex, sepal horns, leaf prickles, and capsule prickles matter more.
argemone-albiflora-subsp-texana.family_connection: The showy petals and many stamens fit the poppy-family pattern, while the prickly vegetative parts help at species level.

phyllotaxy.plain: The pattern of leaves around a stem.
phyllotaxy.formal: The arrangement of leaves on an axis.
phyllotaxy.where: Trace one stem and look at where successive leaves attach.
phyllotaxy.why: Alternate, opposite, and whorled leaves can immediately narrow an ID.

alternate.plain: One leaf attaches at each node, with the leaves alternating positions as you move up the stem.
alternate.formal: A phyllotactic pattern with a single leaf at each node.
alternate.where: Follow the stem node by node. If you find only one leaf at each node rather than a pair, the arrangement is alternate.
alternate.why: Alternate versus opposite is one of the fastest vegetative characters for narrowing plant identity.

real_photo.label: Alternate leaves — one leaf at each node
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Salix babylonica showing alternate leaves along a twig
real_photo.focus: Trace the twig upward. Each node carries one leaf, and the next leaf occurs at a different position farther up the stem.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

opposite.plain: Two leaves attach at the same node directly across from one another.
opposite.formal: A phyllotactic pattern with paired leaves at each node.
opposite.where: Find a node and check whether two leaves leave the stem at the same level on opposite sides.
opposite.why: Opposite versus alternate is a major first-pass field character even when flowers are absent.

real_photo.label: Opposite leaves — two leaves sharing one node
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Tetradenia riparia showing opposite leaf pairs and decussate phyllotaxis
real_photo.focus: Choose one node and look across the stem. The two leaves attached at the same level form an opposite pair.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the source description explicitly identifies the leaves as opposite and decussate.

whorled.plain: Three or more leaves attach around the stem at the same node.
whorled.formal: A phyllotactic pattern with three or more appendages at a node.
whorled.where: Pick one node and count how many leaves radiate from that single level.
whorled.why: A true whorl is visually distinctive and can rapidly narrow the plant group.

real_photo.label: Whorled leaves radiating from one node
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Galium aparine showing leaves arranged in a whorl
real_photo.focus: Look at one stem junction and count the leaf-like structures radiating around it. Several arise at the same level, forming a whorl.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

petiole.plain: The petiole is the leaf stalk connecting the blade to the stem.
petiole.formal: The stalk attaching a leaf blade to the stem.
petiole.where: Start at the leaf blade and trace inward toward the stem. The narrow stalk between them is the petiole.
petiole.why: Whether a leaf has a petiole — and its length, shape, wings or hairs — can be diagnostic.

real_photo.label: Petiole connecting a leaf to the stem
real_photo.alt: Close real photograph of Oenanthe lachenalii showing the stem and petiole
real_photo.focus: Follow the leaf toward the stem. The stalk-like connection between the leaf blade and the stem is the petiole.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the Wikimedia Commons source specifically identifies this as a stem-and-petiole close-up.

sessile.plain: A sessile leaf attaches directly to the stem without a petiole.
sessile.where: Look at the base of the leaf. If the blade reaches the stem directly with no stalk in between, it is sessile.
sessile.why: Petiole present versus absent is an easy, repeatable character for separating similar plants.

real_photo.label: Sessile leaf — no petiole between blade and stem
real_photo.alt: Close real photograph of Galium aparine leaves, which are sessile at the stem
real_photo.focus: Follow one leaf all the way to the stem. There is no narrow leaf stalk between the blade and its attachment point.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the source description identifies these leaves as sessile.

pubescent.plain: Pubescent means a plant surface is covered with hairs.
pubescent.formal: Bearing trichomes or hairs on a plant surface.
pubescent.where: Use side light or a hand lens on the leaf, stem, bud or fruit. Look for tiny hairs projecting from the surface.
pubescent.why: Hair presence, density, direction and texture can separate species that otherwise look very similar.

real_photo.label: Pubescent leaf surface with trichomes visible
real_photo.credit: Brandon Antonio Segura Torres & Priscilla Vieto Bonilla · CC BY-SA 4.0
real_photo.alt: Close cross-section photograph of a pubescent leaf showing projecting trichomes
real_photo.focus: Look along the outside edge of the leaf. The projecting hair-like structures are trichomes; together they make the surface pubescent.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

glabrous.plain: Glabrous means the plant surface has no hairs.
glabrous.where: Inspect the surface under side light and compare it with a nearby hairy surface if possible. A glabrous surface lacks projecting trichomes.
glabrous.why: Hairless versus pubescent is a simple but often decisive species-level character.

real_photo.label: Glabrous leaf surface — no hairs
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of a smooth glabrous Melochia villosissima leaf
real_photo.focus: Scan the leaf surface and margin. There are no visible hairs projecting from the surface; that hairless condition is glabrous.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the Wikimedia Commons source specifically describes this leaf as glabrous.

lanceolate.plain: Lanceolate means lance-shaped: much longer than wide, widest below the middle, and tapering toward the tip.
lanceolate.formal: Lance-shaped; narrowly ovate with the widest portion below the midpoint.
lanceolate.where: Ignore small damaged leaves and look at a mature blade from directly above. Compare its widest point with the middle of the leaf.
lanceolate.why: Leaf shape becomes useful when combined with arrangement, attachment, margin and surface characters.

real_photo.label: Lanceolate leaf — long, narrow, widest below the middle
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a Plantago lanceolata leaf showing a lanceolate outline
real_photo.focus: Trace the outline from base to tip. The blade is much longer than wide and narrows gradually toward both ends, with the broadest zone below midleaf.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

ovate.plain: Ovate means egg-shaped, with the broadest part of the blade below the middle and toward the base.
ovate.formal: Broadly egg-shaped in outline, widest below the middle.
ovate.where: Look at the whole mature leaf from directly above and find where it is widest.
ovate.why: Ovate is a very common key term, but it works best when paired with apex, base, margin and attachment characters.

real_photo.label: Ovate leaf — broader toward the base
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a birch leaf showing an ovate overall outline
real_photo.focus: Follow the blade outline. The lower half is broader than the upper half, producing the egg-shaped ovate form.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the same source photograph was used on Wikimedia Commons to illustrate ovate leaf shape.

rhizome.plain: A rhizome is a horizontal stem, usually underground, that can produce roots and new shoots from its nodes.
rhizome.formal: A usually horizontal subterranean stem bearing nodes, buds, and roots.
rhizome.where: When a plant forms a colony, look at exposed or naturally disturbed soil for a thick horizontal stem connecting shoots. Do not dig up plants just to check.
rhizome.why: Recognizing a rhizome explains how many perennials spread and tells you that the underground structure is a stem, not simply a root.

real_photo.label: Rhizome with roots and shoot buds
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of an Alpinia purpurata rhizome showing thick horizontal stem tissue, roots and shoot buds
real_photo.focus: The thick fleshy axis is the rhizome. Notice roots emerging from it and pointed buds/shoots arising from the stem tissue.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

capitulum.plain: A capitulum is the whole composite flower head — what looks like one sunflower 'flower' is actually many small florets packed together.
capitulum.formal: A compact inflorescence of sessile florets on a common receptacle.
capitulum.where: Look at the entire sunflower-family head first, then mentally separate the outer ray florets from the central disc florets.
capitulum.why: Recognizing the capitulum is the basic move that makes Asteraceae morphology much easier to understand.

real_photo.label: Common sunflower capitulum — many florets forming one head
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of a common sunflower head
real_photo.focus: The entire circular structure — rays plus center — is one capitulum made of many individual florets.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing Rifat R CC BY 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph; the underlying source image is unmodified.

phyllary.plain: A phyllary is one individual bract in the green wrapping around the base of an Asteraceae flower head.
phyllary.formal: A modified bract forming part of the involucre beneath a capitulum.
phyllary.where: Turn the head sideways or look at a bud. Pick out one scale- or leaf-like unit beneath the florets.
phyllary.why: Phyllary number, rows, hairs, shape and whether the tips spread or press inward can separate similar genera and species.

real_photo.label: Real Asteraceae phyllaries around a developing head
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of overlapping phyllaries around an Asteraceae flower bud
real_photo.focus: Pick one individual overlapping bract. One unit is a phyllary; all of them together form the involucre.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing RoRo CC0 photograph; the underlying source image is unmodified.

involucre.plain: The involucre is the complete set of phyllaries wrapped around the base of a flower head.
involucre.formal: A whorl or series of bracts subtending an inflorescence.
involucre.where: Look beneath the florets and take in the whole green bract layer rather than one individual scale.
involucre.why: Overall involucre shape and phyllary arrangement are often stronger ID characters than flower color.

real_photo.label: Real Asteraceae involucre
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of the ring of phyllaries forming an Asteraceae involucre
real_photo.focus: The entire ring or cluster of overlapping phyllaries is the involucre. A single unit within it is one phyllary.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same RoRo CC0 photograph as the Phyllary lesson, with the overlay shifted from one part to the whole structure.

ray-floret.plain: A ray floret is an individual flower with a strap-like corolla that looks like one big petal.
ray-floret.formal: A zygomorphic floret with an expanded ligulate corolla, often at the margin of an Asteraceae head.
ray-floret.where: Look around the outer edge of a daisy- or sunflower-like head. Each strap-like unit belongs to its own floret.
ray-floret.why: Ray-floret presence, number, size and shape are useful Asteraceae characters — and remembering that each 'petal' is a flower prevents a major morphology mistake.

real_photo.label: Real ray florets on Helianthus annuus
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of a common sunflower showing peripheral ray florets
real_photo.focus: Pick one yellow strap around the edge. That strap belongs to one ray floret; it is not merely one petal of a single giant flower.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing Rifat R CC BY 4.0 sunflower photograph; the underlying source image is unmodified.

disc-floret.plain: A disc floret is one tiny tubular flower packed into the center of many Asteraceae flower heads.
disc-floret.formal: A usually actinomorphic tubular floret of the disc portion of a capitulum.
disc-floret.where: Move your eye into the center of a sunflower-like head and isolate one repeated tubular unit rather than viewing the center as one solid disc.
disc-floret.why: Disc-floret shape, color and reproductive details can help separate Asteraceae groups.

real_photo.label: Real disk florets on Helianthus annuus
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of a common sunflower showing central disk florets
real_photo.focus: The center is made of many separate tiny flowers. Pick one repeated tubular unit: that is one disc floret.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same Rifat R CC BY 4.0 sunflower photograph as the Capitulum and Ray floret lessons, with the overlay focused on one central flower.

receptacle.plain: The receptacle is the platform that supports the florets in a flower head.
receptacle.formal: The expanded axis bearing floral organs or, in Asteraceae, the florets of the capitulum.
receptacle.where: In Asteraceae, look underneath the florets. After florets or fruits fall away, the exposed platform is easiest to see.
receptacle.why: A smooth, pitted, hairy, or scale-bearing receptacle can be an important Asteraceae character.

real_photo.label: Dandelion receptacle after the fruits have dispersed
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of the exposed receptacle of a dandelion after seed dispersal
real_photo.focus: The exposed central platform is the receptacle. The florets and fruits were attached across this surface.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY 4.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

pappus.plain: The pappus is the tuft, bristles, scales or awns attached to the top of an Asteraceae fruit.
pappus.formal: A modified calyx borne at the apex of an Asteraceae cypsela.
pappus.where: Inspect a mature fruit after flowering. Look above the dry fruit body for a parachute-like tuft or other modified calyx structure.
pappus.why: Pappus form is often a strong genus- or species-level character in Asteraceae.

real_photo.label: Real dandelion pappus attached to the fruit
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of a dandelion fruit with its fine hair-like pappus
real_photo.focus: The fine parachute-like hairs are the pappus. The dry fruit body below them is the cypsela.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing Tagooty CC BY-SA 4.0 dandelion fruit photograph; the underlying source image is unmodified.

cypsela.plain: A cypsela is the dry one-seeded fruit produced by one Asteraceae floret.
cypsela.formal: A dry indehiscent one-seeded fruit derived from an inferior ovary.
cypsela.where: Look below the pappus for the solid dry fruit body. That lower body — not the fluffy tuft — is the cypsela.
cypsela.why: Cypsela shape, ribs, hairs and its relationship to the pappus can confirm difficult Asteraceae identifications.

real_photo.label: Real Asteraceae one-seeded fruit with pappus
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of a dandelion fruit attached to a pappus
real_photo.focus: The lower dry seed-like body is the cypsela. The hair-like parachute above it is the pappus.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same Tagooty CC BY-SA 4.0 dandelion fruit photograph as the Pappus lesson, with the overlay shifted to the fruit body.

latex.plain: Latex is a distinctive plant exudate that may be milky, clear, colored or sticky.
latex.formal: A complex cellular exudate produced in laticifers.
latex.where: Only observe latex from existing damage whenever possible. On many Euphorbia and milkweeds it appears immediately at a broken or cut surface.
latex.why: Sap type can be highly diagnostic, but it is a supporting character and should not be tested by unnecessarily injuring plants.

real_photo.label: Milky Euphorbia latex at a damaged surface
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of white latex exuding from a Euphorbia
real_photo.focus: The opaque white liquid emerging from the damaged tissue is latex.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

umbel.plain: An umbel is a flower cluster whose individual stalks spread from about the same point, like umbrella ribs.
umbel.formal: An inflorescence with pedicels arising from a common point.
umbel.where: Step back and look at the whole cluster. Follow the flower stalks inward and see whether they converge at one central point.
umbel.why: Umbel architecture is a fast way to understand milkweed clusters and many other inflorescences.

real_photo.label: Milkweed umbel-like flower cluster
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of an Asclepias verticillata flower cluster showing stalks radiating from a common point
real_photo.focus: Trace several flower stalks inward. They converge near one point, producing the umbrella-like umbel pattern.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY 3.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

corona.plain: The corona is the extra crown-like structure in the center of a milkweed flower; in Asclepias it is made of five hoods and their associated horns.
corona.formal: An appendage or series of appendages between the corolla and stamens.
corona.where: Ignore the reflexed petals first. Look inside them at the five-part crown surrounding the central reproductive column.
corona.why: The size, shape, color and arrangement of the corona — especially hoods and horns — are among the most useful milkweed characters.

real_photo.label: Real Asclepias asperula flower
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of Asclepias asperula flower
real_photo.focus: The corona is the entire five-part crown around the flower center. Each broad hood is one part of that crown.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons macro; the underlying source image is unmodified.

gynostegium.plain: The gynostegium is the fused central reproductive column of a milkweed flower.
gynostegium.formal: A reproductive complex formed by fusion/close union of anthers with the stigmatic head.
gynostegium.where: Look at the very center of the flower, inside the five corona hoods. The central column with the stigmatic slits is the gynostegium.
gynostegium.why: This fused structure is one of the defining milkweed features and is where the pollinaria attach and are removed by visiting insects.

real_photo.label: Real Asclepias asperula flower cross-section
real_photo.alt: Cross section photograph of Asclepias asperula flower
real_photo.focus: The central fused column is the gynostegium. The corona hoods surround it but are not part of the gynostegium.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons cross-section; the underlying source image is unmodified.

hood.plain: A hood is one of the five broad cup- or pouch-shaped parts of a milkweed corona.
hood.formal: A cucullate corona segment in Asclepias, often associated with an internal horn.
hood.where: Look around the center of the flower for five repeated cup-like structures. Pick one broad unit: that is a hood.
hood.why: Hood shape, height, color and position relative to the gynostegium are important for separating milkweed species.

real_photo.label: Real hood structures on Asclepias asperula
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of Asclepias asperula flower
real_photo.focus: Pick one of the five broad cup-like corona segments. That single broad structure is one hood.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons macro; the underlying source image is unmodified.

horn.plain: A horn is the narrower projection that rises from inside a milkweed hood.
horn.formal: A cornu arising from the interior of a corona hood in many Asclepias.
horn.where: After finding a hood, look inside it for a narrower finger-, hook-, or horn-like projection pointing inward or upward.
horn.why: Horn length, curvature, position and whether it projects beyond the hood can be decisive in Asclepias identification.

real_photo.label: Real horn structures on Asclepias asperula
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of Asclepias asperula flower
real_photo.focus: First find the broad hood, then look inside it for the narrower projection. That inner projection is the horn.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons macro; the underlying source image is unmodified.

pollinium.plain: A pollinium is one coherent packet of pollen that moves as a single unit.
pollinium.formal: A coherent mass of pollen grains transferred together during pollination.
pollinium.where: In a removed milkweed pollinarium, look for the two larger pollen masses connected by thin translator arms to a tiny central clip called the corpusculum.
pollinium.why: Milkweeds move pollen in packages rather than as loose grains, so recognizing the pollinium explains both their flower structure and their unusual pollination mechanism.

real_photo.label: Real Asclepias asperula pollinarium
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of Asclepias asperula pollinarium
real_photo.focus: One larger pollen mass on either side is a pollinium. The pair plus the central connector structures make the pollinarium.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons macro; the underlying source image is unmodified.

follicle.plain: A follicle is a dry fruit that opens along one seam. A milkweed 'pod' is a follicle.
follicle.formal: A dry dehiscent fruit derived from one carpel and opening along a single suture.
follicle.where: Look at a mature milkweed fruit from the side and find the long seam where it will split open.
follicle.why: Follicle size, shape, orientation and surface texture can support milkweed identification, especially after flowering.

real_photo.label: Real Asclepias tuberosa follicle
real_photo.alt: Photograph of an Asclepias tuberosa follicle
real_photo.focus: The whole pod-like structure is one follicle. Follow the long edge to find the single opening seam, or suture.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing H. Zell CC BY-SA 3.0 image already stored in the Asclepias tuberosa learner package.

cupule.plain: The cupule is the cap-like cup at the base of an acorn.
cupule.formal: A cup-like involucre of bract-derived tissue subtending or partially enclosing the nut in Fagaceae.
cupule.where: Look at the scaly cup or cap attached to the base of the acorn.
cupule.why: Cupule depth, shape, surface and scale characters are useful when comparing oaks.

real_photo.label: Cupule holding the base of an oak acorn
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of an English oak acorn showing the cupule around its base
real_photo.focus: The scaly cap gripping the base of the acorn is the cupule. The smooth structure projecting from it is the nut.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

catkin.plain: A catkin is a slender cluster of many tiny, usually inconspicuous flowers, often hanging from a twig.
catkin.formal: A usually pendent spike-like inflorescence of small unisexual flowers.
catkin.where: On oaks, look in spring for dangling pollen-producing clusters emerging near the new leaves.
catkin.why: Catkins help you recognize the reproductive architecture of oaks and other wind-pollinated woody plants.

real_photo.label: Oak catkins — many tiny flowers on hanging axes
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of oak catkins hanging from a twig
real_photo.focus: Do not look for one showy flower. Follow one dangling axis: the many tiny flowers arranged along it together make the catkin.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the Wikimedia Commons source identifies these structures as oak catkins.

cyathium.plain: A cyathium is a tiny cup-like Euphorbia inflorescence that looks like one flower but contains highly reduced male and female flowers.
cyathium.formal: A specialized pseudanthium with a central female flower and reduced male flowers enclosed by an involucre with glands.
cyathium.where: Use a macro view. Look for the cup-like involucre, nectar glands, and tiny reproductive flowers within the unit.
cyathium.why: Recognizing the cyathium is the key step to understanding Euphorbia flower-like structures.

real_photo.label: Real Euphorbia cyathium in macro view
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of Euphorbia milii showing a cyathium
real_photo.focus: The entire central flower-like unit is one cyathium. The showy surrounding structures are not ordinary petals.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons macro.

corolla.plain: The corolla is all of a flower’s petals considered together.
corolla.formal: The inner, usually showy whorl of the perianth, composed of petals.
corolla.where: Find the calyx first, then move inward to the usually colored petal tissue. All of that petal tissue together is the corolla.
corolla.why: Corolla fusion, symmetry, tube length and lobing are major family- and genus-level characters.

real_photo.label: Real Monarda corolla from the side
real_photo.alt: Close side-view photograph of a Monarda didyma corolla
real_photo.focus: Follow the colored fused petal tissue of one flower. All of that petal tissue together is the corolla.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing Alex Abair CC BY 4.0 Monarda photograph.

calyx.plain: All the sepals together—the outer floral covering below the petals.
calyx.formal: The outer whorl of the perianth, composed of sepals.
calyx.where: Look directly below or outside the corolla.
calyx.why: Sepal shape and surface are important in morning-glories and many other groups.

real_photo.alt: Close photograph of Jasminum sambac flower buds showing the green sepals surrounding the base of each bud
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.
real_photo.label: Calyx = the complete outer whorl of sepals
real_photo.focus: On the right-hand bud, follow the whole green whorl surrounding the base of the white corolla. All of those sepals together are the calyx.

sepal.plain: One individual part of the calyx.
sepal.formal: A member of the outer perianth whorl.
sepal.why: Shape, length, horns, hairs, and persistence can be diagnostic.

real_photo.alt: Close photograph of Jasminum sambac flower buds showing the green sepals surrounding the base of each bud
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.
real_photo.label: Sepal = one individual member of the calyx
real_photo.focus: On the right-hand bud, isolate one narrow green lobe. That single lobe is a sepal; the complete set is the calyx.

sympetalous.plain: Sympetalous means the petals are fused together for at least part of their length.
sympetalous.formal: Having connate petals forming a corolla tube.
sympetalous.where: Look for a continuous corolla tube rather than petals that are completely separate all the way to the base.
sympetalous.why: Fused petals create many diagnostic corolla shapes, including funnels, bells and two-lipped tubes.

real_photo.label: Fused-petal Monarda corolla
real_photo.alt: Real side-view photograph of a Monarda didyma flower showing a fused corolla tube
real_photo.focus: The colored petal tissue is joined into a continuous tube before dividing into lobes. That fusion makes the corolla sympetalous.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same CC BY 4.0 Monarda photograph as the Corolla lesson, with the overlay focused on petal fusion.

capsule.plain: A capsule is a dry fruit that opens at maturity to release its seeds.
capsule.formal: A dry dehiscent fruit derived from a compound ovary.
capsule.where: Look at mature fruit after the petals are gone. Find the dry fruit wall and the seams or valves where it opens.
capsule.why: Capsules vary in shape and opening pattern, and those differences are often diagnostic.

real_photo.label: Opened capsule revealing seeds
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of an opened Swietenia mahagoni capsule revealing winged seeds
real_photo.focus: The dry outer fruit has split open into valves. The structure before opening is the capsule; the exposed structures inside are seeds.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

culm.plain: A culm is the stem of a grass.
culm.formal: The aerial stem of a grass, commonly jointed into nodes and internodes.
culm.where: Look for the main stem axis running upward between the leaf sheaths.
culm.why: Once you can separate culm, node, sheath, blade and ligule, grass structure becomes much easier to read.

real_photo.label: Grass culm with node and sheaths visible
real_photo.alt: Annotated photograph of Timothy grass showing blade, ligule, sheath, node and exposed culm
real_photo.focus: Find the exposed stem segment between the leaf sheaths. That main stem is the culm.
real_photo.annotation_note: The source photo already contains numbered labels; the learner overlay adds plain-language arrows. Source labels: 1 = blade · 2 = ligule · 3 = upper sheath · 4 = node · 5 = exposed culm · 6 = sheath.

node.plain: A node is the joint on a grass stem where a leaf attaches.
node.formal: A stem region from which one or more appendages such as leaves or branches arise.
node.where: Look for the knuckle-like joint along the culm.
node.why: Nodes are one of the main landmarks on grasses and help separate stem segments from the leaf parts attached to them.

real_photo.label: Grass node on the culm
real_photo.alt: Annotated photograph of Timothy grass showing the node and exposed culm
real_photo.focus: Find the swollen joint where the leaf attaches to the stem. That joint is the node.
real_photo.annotation_note: The source photo already contains numbered labels; the learner overlay isolates the node. Source label 4 = node and 5 = exposed culm.

leaf-sheath.plain: The lower part of a grass leaf that wraps around the stem.
leaf-sheath.formal: The basal, usually tubular or open portion of a leaf surrounding the culm.
leaf-sheath.where: Below the blade, wrapped around the grass stem.
leaf-sheath.why: Sheath characters are part of the standard vegetative grass-ID toolkit.

real_photo.annotation_note: The source photo already has numbered labels; learner arrows add plain-language reinforcement.
real_photo.label: Annotated real grass leaf sheath
real_photo.alt: Annotated photograph of Timothy grass showing upper and lower leaf sheaths
real_photo.focus: The lower leaf portion wrapping the culm is the sheath. Compare it with the exposed culm and the blade above.

collar.plain: The collar is the band or zone where a grass leaf blade meets the sheath.
collar.formal: The external region at the blade-sheath junction, opposite the ligule.
collar.where: Look on the outside of the grass leaf where the blade joins the sheath.
collar.why: The collar region, together with the ligule and sheath, is one of the first places to check in grass identification.

real_photo.label: Grass collar at the blade-sheath junction
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of Panicum capillare showing the collar, sheath, node and hairy ligule region
real_photo.focus: Find the narrow transition zone where the blade meets the sheath. That band is the collar; nearby hairs and the ligule are separate features.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

ligule.plain: A tiny membrane, fringe of hairs or similar structure on the inside of a grass leaf where blade meets sheath.
ligule.formal: An appendage at the adaxial blade-sheath junction in many grasses.
ligule.where: Inside the leaf collar, between blade and culm.
ligule.why: Ligule type and length are often species- or genus-level characters.

real_photo.label: Real grass ligule with arrow
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of a grass ligule with an arrow pointing to the ligule
real_photo.focus: Find the tiny appendage on the inside of the blade–sheath junction. That is the ligule.
real_photo.annotation_note: The source photograph already contains an arrow; learner overlay adds a plain-language label.

spikelet.plain: The small flowering unit you should isolate when identifying a grass.
spikelet.formal: A grass inflorescence unit containing one or more florets, usually subtended by glumes.
spikelet.where: Pick one unit from the grass inflorescence rather than studying the whole panicle at once.
spikelet.why: Most reproductive grass characters live at the spikelet/floret scale.

real_photo.label: Annotated real grass spikelet
real_photo.alt: Annotated photograph of a Triticum spelta spikelet with glume, lemma, and palea labels
real_photo.focus: Treat the entire reproductive unit as one spikelet. The embedded source labels identify glume, lemma and palea inside it.
real_photo.annotation_note: Source labels remain visible; learner arrows emphasize whole-unit versus internal parts.

glume.plain: One of the bracts at the base of many grass spikelets.
glume.formal: A sterile bract, commonly one of a basal pair, subtending the florets of a grass spikelet.
glume.where: At the outside/base of an isolated spikelet.
glume.why: Glume size, veins, keels and awns are important grass characters.

real_photo.label: Real spikelet with glume labeled
real_photo.alt: Annotated photograph of a Triticum spelta spikelet with glume, lemma, and palea labels
real_photo.focus: The glume is the outer basal bract of the spikelet. Find the source label “Glu” and compare it with the whole spikelet.
real_photo.annotation_note: Source labels remain visible; learner overlay isolates the glume.

lemma.plain: The outer of the two main bracts enclosing a grass floret.
lemma.formal: The lower/outer bract of a grass floret, often bearing an awn.
lemma.where: Inside the glumes, around each floret.
lemma.why: Lemma shape, texture and awns are central to grass identification.

real_photo.label: Real spikelet with lemma labeled
real_photo.alt: Annotated photograph of a Triticum spelta spikelet with glume, lemma, and palea labels
real_photo.focus: The lemma sits inside the glumes and encloses the floret from the outside. Find the source label “Lem”.
real_photo.annotation_note: Source labels remain visible; learner overlay isolates lemma versus glume.

palea.plain: The inner bract paired with the lemma around a grass floret.
palea.formal: The upper/inner bract enclosing the grass flower opposite the lemma.
palea.where: Inside a floret, tucked against the lemma.
palea.why: Lemma + palea define the floret envelope used in technical grass ID.

real_photo.label: Real spikelet with palea labeled
real_photo.alt: Annotated photograph of a Triticum spelta spikelet with glume, lemma, and palea labels
real_photo.focus: The palea is the inner bract paired against the lemma around a floret. Find the source label “Pal”.
real_photo.annotation_note: Source labels remain visible; learner overlay emphasizes palea versus lemma.

awn.plain: An awn is a thin bristle-like extension sticking out from a grass spikelet part, often the lemma.
awn.formal: A slender bristle-like appendage, commonly arising from a lemma or glume.
awn.where: Look for a stiff or hairlike bristle projecting from a spikelet; it may be straight, bent or twisted.
awn.why: Presence, absence, number, length, position and shape of awns can quickly separate similar grasses.

real_photo.label: Grass spikelet with awns visible
real_photo.alt: Hand-lens photograph of an Aira caryophyllea spikelet showing bent awns
real_photo.focus: Look for the thin bristle-like projections extending from the spikelet. Those projecting bristles are awns.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

stipule.plain: A stipule is a small leaf-like appendage at the base of a leaf.
stipule.formal: One of a pair of appendages associated with the leaf base in many angiosperms.
stipule.where: Look right where the petiole meets the stem; stipules are usually beside that leaf base.
stipule.why: Whether stipules are present, absent, fused, spiny, tiny or conspicuous can be an important family or genus character.

real_photo.label: Paired stipules beside a Euphorbia leaf base
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of Euphorbia hypericifolia showing small stipules at the leaf base
real_photo.focus: Ignore the larger leaf blade and look at the tiny pointed appendages beside the point where the leaf attaches to the stem.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

pulvinus.plain: A pulvinus is a swollen, joint-like region at the base of a leaf or leaflet that allows movement or flexing.
pulvinus.formal: A specialized motor or flexible swelling at the base of a petiole, petiolule or leaflet.
pulvinus.where: Look at the base of the petiole or leaflet stalk for a visibly thickened joint.
pulvinus.why: Pulvini are common in Fabaceae and help explain leaf movement in plants such as Mimosa.

real_photo.label: Sensitive-plant illustration showing the pulvinus
real_photo.credit: Alfred Barton Rendle / Encyclopædia Britannica 1911 · public domain
real_photo.alt: Historical botanical illustration of Mimosa pudica showing leaf movement and the pulvinus
real_photo.focus: The swollen joint marked p in the source illustration is the pulvinus. It changes position as the leaf moves.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain botanical illustration that explicitly labels the pulvinus.

legume.plain: A legume is the characteristic Fabaceae fruit: a pod derived from one carpel, often opening along two seams.
legume.formal: A dry or modified fruit derived from a single carpel, classically dehiscing along two sutures.
legume.where: Look at a mature bean- or pea-like pod and follow the two margins from base to tip.
legume.why: The one-carpel pod is the strongest fruit-level structural thread connecting the pea family.

real_photo.label: Opened bean legume showing seeds and pod valves
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of an opened Phaseolus vulgaris bean pod containing mature seeds
real_photo.focus: The entire pod is one legume. It opens into two valves, exposing seeds attached along the fruit margin.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons photograph.

superior-ovary.plain: A superior ovary sits above the point where the sepals, petals and stamens attach.
superior-ovary.formal: An ovary with the other floral whorls inserted below it.
superior-ovary.where: Use a side view or section. Find the ovary first, then trace where the other flower parts join relative to it.
superior-ovary.why: Ovary position is one of the strongest family-level floral characters.

real_photo.label: Superior versus inferior ovary comparison
real_photo.alt: Botanical comparison illustration showing a superior ovary on the left and inferior ovary on the right
real_photo.focus: Use the left-hand flower. The ovary is above the attachment level of the petals, sepals and stamens.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons comparison illustration.

papilionoid.plain: Papilionoid describes the classic pea-flower arrangement: one large standard, two side wings, and two lower petals forming the keel.
papilionoid.formal: A zygomorphic corolla architecture typical of many Papilionoideae, with standard, wing and keel petals.
papilionoid.where: View the flower from the front and side. Find the large upper petal first, then the two wings and the lower keel.
papilionoid.why: This flower form is extremely useful within Fabaceae, but not every legume has it.

real_photo.label: Papilionoid pea flower — standard, wings, and keel
real_photo.alt: Public-domain botanical illustration of a pea flower showing standard, wing, keel, and calyx
real_photo.focus: The large upper petal is the standard, the side petals are wings, and the two lower petals form the keel.
real_photo.annotation_note: The source illustration already labels the major papilionoid petal regions; learner overlay reinforces the field terms.

decussate.plain: Decussate means the leaves are opposite, but each new pair is rotated about 90° from the pair above and below.
decussate.formal: An opposite phyllotactic pattern in which successive pairs are arranged at right angles.
decussate.where: Look across at least three nodes. First confirm opposite pairs, then see whether successive pairs cross at right angles.
decussate.why: This repeated cross-like pattern is especially useful in many mint-family plants and other opposite-leaved groups.

real_photo.label: Decussate — successive opposite pairs rotated 90°
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Tetradenia riparia showing successive opposite leaf pairs rotated at right angles
real_photo.focus: Compare one opposite pair with the pair immediately above it. The next pair is rotated roughly 90°, creating the decussate pattern.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same source photo as the Opposite lesson, but the overlay shifts attention from one pair to the rotation between successive pairs.

bilabiate.plain: Bilabiate means the corolla is shaped into two lips: an upper lip and a lower lip.
bilabiate.formal: A zygomorphic perianth or corolla divided into two lip-like portions.
bilabiate.where: View the flower from the front or side. Look for one group of corolla lobes forming an upper lip and another forming a lower landing-platform-like lip.
bilabiate.why: Two-lipped flowers are common in Lamiaceae and several lookalike families, so this is useful when combined with ovary and fruit characters.

real_photo.label: Bilabiate Salvia corolla
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of Salvia officinalis flowers showing the upper and lower lips of the corolla
real_photo.focus: Pick one flower and separate the upper corolla lip from the larger lower lip. Together they make the flower bilabiate.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 2.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

gynobasic-style.plain: A gynobasic style rises from low between the lobes of the ovary instead of from the ovary tip.
gynobasic-style.formal: A style inserted near the base or between lobes of a deeply divided ovary.
gynobasic-style.where: In a dissected mint-family flower, find the four ovary lobes and then look for the style emerging from the center between them.
gynobasic-style.why: This is one of the most useful structural clues for understanding classic Lamiaceae flower architecture.

real_photo.label: Real dissected Salvia showing a gynobasic style
real_photo.alt: Dissected Salvia aurea flower showing the gynobasic style rising between four ovary lobes
real_photo.focus: The style rises from low between the four ovary lobes. That low central origin is what makes it gynobasic.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing SAplants CC BY-SA 4.0 dissected Salvia photograph.

nutlet.plain: A nutlet is a small dry one-seeded fruit unit. In many mints, one flower can produce four nutlets.
nutlet.formal: A small indehiscent one-seeded unit, often one of several produced by a schizocarpic ovary.
nutlet.where: After the corolla falls, look inside the persistent calyx. Mature Lamiaceae fruits often separate into four small nutlets.
nutlet.why: The four-nutlet pattern is a classic fruit character in Lamiaceae and several related groups.

real_photo.label: Four nutlets inside a Salvia fruiting calyx
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph looking into a Salvia sclarea fruit showing four nutlets
real_photo.focus: Look inside the fruiting structure. The four separate small dry units are nutlets.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

persistent-calyx.plain: A persistent calyx is a set of sepals that stays attached after the petals fall and remains around the developing fruit.
persistent-calyx.formal: A calyx retained through fruit development.
persistent-calyx.where: Look at a plant after flowering. If the calyx is still wrapped around or beneath the fruit, it is persistent.
persistent-calyx.why: A retained calyx is a useful clue in Lamiaceae, Solanaceae and many other families.

real_photo.label: Persistent Salvia calyces around developing nutlets
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Salvia aurea calyces retained around developing nutlets
real_photo.focus: The corolla is gone, but the calyx remains around the developing fruit. That retained floral structure is a persistent calyx.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

staminal-column.plain: A staminal column is a tube formed when many stamen filaments fuse around the style.
staminal-column.formal: A columnar androecial structure produced by fusion of stamen filaments, conspicuous in many Malvoideae.
staminal-column.where: Look in the center of a mallow flower. The long central column bearing many anthers is the staminal column.
staminal-column.why: A conspicuous staminal column is one of the most useful visual clues for many Malvoideae.

real_photo.label: Hibiscus staminal column with many anthers
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of a Hibiscus flower showing many anthers borne along the staminal column
real_photo.focus: The long central tube supporting many yellow anthers is the staminal column. The style runs through its center and extends beyond it.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

stellate-hair.plain: A stellate hair is a trichome with several arms radiating from one center like a tiny star.
stellate-hair.formal: A branched trichome whose rays arise from a common center.
stellate-hair.where: Use a hand lens or microscope on leaves, stems or calyces. Do not just ask whether the surface is hairy — look at the shape of an individual hair.
stellate-hair.why: Stellate hairs are a useful supporting clue in many Malvaceae and help distinguish types of pubescence.

real_photo.label: Stellate trichome — several rays from one center
real_photo.alt: Botanical diagram of a sessile stellate trichome with several rays radiating from one center
real_photo.focus: All of the arms belong to one trichome. Their shared central attachment creates the star-shaped, stellate form.
real_photo.annotation_note: This is a public-domain structure diagram used because individual stellate hairs are usually too small for ordinary field photographs.

epicalyx.plain: An epicalyx is an extra ring of bracts immediately outside the true calyx.
epicalyx.formal: A whorl or series of bracts immediately subtending and resembling an additional calyx.
epicalyx.where: View the flower from the side. Find the sepals first, then look just outside or below them for a second calyx-like ring of bracts.
epicalyx.why: An epicalyx is common in many mallows and can be a strong supporting character, but some Malvaceae lack one.

real_photo.label: Malvaceae flower showing calyx and epicalyx
real_photo.alt: Real side-view photograph of a Malvaceae flower showing the true calyx and an outer epicalyx
real_photo.focus: Find the true calyx around the flower base, then look immediately outside it. The extra outer bracts form the epicalyx.
