real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 2.0 source photograph; the source itself is titled as showing calyx and epicalyx.

schizocarp.plain: A schizocarp is a dry fruit that splits at maturity into separate fruit segments called mericarps.
schizocarp.formal: A dry fruit derived from a compound ovary that separates into mericarps.
schizocarp.where: Look at a mature segmented fruit. First recognize the whole fruit, then see whether it is built from repeated sections that can separate.
schizocarp.why: Schizocarps are common in mallows and several other families; recognizing the whole-fruit architecture makes mericarp terminology much easier.

real_photo.label: Abutilon schizocarp built from many mericarps
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of an Abutilon theophrasti fruit composed of fourteen mericarps
real_photo.focus: The complete wheel-like fruit is the schizocarp. Each repeated wedge around the edge is one mericarp.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 photograph; the source description identifies fourteen mericarps.

mericarp.plain: A mericarp is one individual segment of a schizocarp.
mericarp.formal: A one-seeded or few-seeded unit into which a schizocarp separates.
mericarp.where: After finding a segmented fruit, isolate one repeated wedge or unit rather than looking at the whole fruit.
mericarp.why: Mericarp number, shape, awns and surface traits are important in many Malvaceae fruits.

real_photo.label: One mericarp within an Abutilon schizocarp
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of an Abutilon theophrasti fruit with many repeated mericarps
real_photo.focus: Pick one repeated wedge around the fruit. That individual segment is a mericarp; all the segments together make the schizocarp.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same CC BY-SA 4.0 Abutilon photograph as the Schizocarp lesson, with the overlay shifted from the whole fruit to one segment.

rosette.plain: A rosette is a tight circular cluster of leaves produced from a very short stem, often close to the ground.
rosette.formal: A compact radial arrangement of leaves with very short internodes.
rosette.where: Look at the whole plant from above. The leaves radiate around a central growing point with little visible stem between them.
rosette.why: Rosette architecture is a powerful first-pass growth-form clue in many unrelated plant groups.

real_photo.label: Basal leaf rosette
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Helminthotheca echioides showing a basal rosette of leaves
real_photo.focus: The leaves radiate from one low central growing point. The short internodes make the cluster look circular and compressed.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons photograph.

tepal.plain: A tepal is a perianth segment used when sepals and petals look too similar to distinguish confidently.
tepal.formal: A perianth segment when calyx and corolla are not differentiated into distinct sepals and petals.
tepal.where: Look at flowers such as tulips, lilies, and yuccas where the outer and inner floral segments look alike.
tepal.why: Tepal terminology avoids forcing similar-looking perianth parts into separate sepal and petal categories.

real_photo.label: Tulip flower with six similar tepals
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a tulip flower showing six similar perianth segments
real_photo.focus: The six showy segments are similar enough in appearance that they are described together as tepals.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons photograph.

terminal-spine.plain: A terminal spine is a stiff hardened point formed at the very tip of a leaf.
terminal-spine.where: Look at the leaf apex without touching it. The large spine directly continuing the leaf tip is terminal.
terminal-spine.why: Terminal-spine size, color, shape, and curvature can help separate Agave, Yucca, and similar rosette plants.

real_photo.label: Agave leaf with terminal spine
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of Agave americana showing the sharp spine at the leaf tip
real_photo.focus: The stiff point at the very end of the leaf is the terminal spine. Smaller teeth along the margin are separate structures.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons close-up, whose source description specifically notes the spike.

achene.plain: An achene is a small dry one-seeded fruit that does not split open at maturity.
achene.formal: A dry indehiscent one-seeded fruit developing from a single carpel or locule.
achene.where: Look at the mature fruit unit itself rather than the seed inside it. On a strawberry, each tiny 'seed-like' speck on the surface is actually an achene.
achene.why: Recognizing the achene as a fruit — not a naked seed — makes aggregate fruits and many Ranunculaceae/Asteraceae structures much easier to understand.

real_photo.label: Real strawberry achenes in macro view
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of a strawberry surface showing individual achenes
real_photo.focus: Each small dry speck on the strawberry surface is one achene. The seed is inside that tiny fruit wall.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing atramos CC BY 2.0 macro photograph.

annotations.label: THESE ARE FRUITS, NOT NAKED SEEDS

petaloid-sepal.plain: A sepal that looks and functions visually like a petal.
petaloid-sepal.formal: A calyx segment enlarged or colored so that it resembles a corolla segment.
petaloid-sepal.where: Look at the showy outer flower parts of Clematis.
petaloid-sepal.why: Prevents mislabeling the showy Clematis perianth as petals.

apocarpous.plain: A flower with separate carpels instead of one fully fused ovary.
apocarpous.formal: A gynoecium composed of two or more unfused carpels.
apocarpous.where: Inspect the flower center or developing aggregate fruit.
apocarpous.why: A strong structural theme in Ranunculaceae.

trifoliolate.plain: Trifoliolate means one compound leaf is made of exactly three leaflets.
trifoliolate.formal: A compound leaf bearing three leaflets.
trifoliolate.where: Do not just count three nearby leaves. Trace all three blades back to one shared petiole to confirm they are leaflets of a single compound leaf.
trifoliolate.why: This is a major field character in poison ivy, fragrant sumac and many legumes.

real_photo.label: Poison ivy trifoliolate leaf — three leaflets in one leaf
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of poison ivy showing a trifoliolate leaf with three leaflets
real_photo.focus: The three blades belong to one compound leaf. Follow them inward to their shared attachment rather than treating them as three separate leaves.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 2.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

odd-pinnate.plain: An odd-pinnate leaf has paired leaflets along the rachis plus one terminal leaflet at the end.
odd-pinnate.formal: A pinnate leaf with paired lateral leaflets and a terminal leaflet.
odd-pinnate.where: Trace the rachis to its tip. If one leaflet sits alone at the very end beyond the lateral pairs, the leaf is odd-pinnate.
odd-pinnate.why: The terminal leaflet separates odd-pinnate leaves from even-pinnate leaves and is common in sumacs and ashes.

real_photo.label: Odd-pinnate architecture — paired leaflets plus a terminal leaflet
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a pinnately compound leaf showing lateral leaflets along a rachis and a terminal leaflet
real_photo.focus: Follow the rachis to the end. The single leaflet at the tip is the terminal leaflet that makes the leaf odd-pinnate.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same CC BY 2.0 source as the Rachis lesson, with the overlay shifted to overall leaf architecture.

rachis.plain: The rachis is the main central axis that continues beyond the petiole through a compound leaf and carries the leaflets.
rachis.formal: A primary axis bearing leaflets, flowers, or other repeated units.
rachis.where: Start at the leaf base. Follow the petiole outward; once leaflet pairs begin, the continuing central axis is the rachis.
rachis.why: Distinguishing petiole from rachis makes compound leaves much easier to read and is essential for characters such as a winged rachis.

real_photo.label: Pinnately compound leaf showing the central rachis
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a pinnately compound leaf with a central rachis carrying multiple leaflets
real_photo.focus: Follow the long central axis between the leaflets. That axis is the rachis; the individual blades attached to it are leaflets.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY 2.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

winged-rachis.plain: A winged rachis has narrow strips of leaf-like tissue running along the sides of the central axis between the leaflets.
winged-rachis.formal: A rachis bordered by longitudinal laminar extensions.
winged-rachis.where: Look between leaflet pairs on a compound sumac leaf. If the rachis itself has flattened green tissue along its sides, it is winged.
winged-rachis.why: A winged rachis is one of the strongest visual clues for winged/flameleaf sumac.

real_photo.label: Winged sumac leaf showing leafy wings along the rachis
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Rhus copallinum showing a compound leaf with narrow green wings along the rachis
real_photo.focus: Ignore the large leaflets for a moment. Look at the central rachis between them; the narrow flattened green tissue along its sides forms the wings.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 3.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

drupe.plain: A drupe is a fleshy fruit with a hard inner stone surrounding the seed.
drupe.formal: A fruit with fleshy exocarp/mesocarp and a hardened endocarp surrounding the seed.
drupe.where: Use a naturally cut or edible fruit when practical. Look from outside inward: skin, fleshy middle, then a hard stone around the seed.
drupe.why: The hard endocarp — the stone — is the key structure separating a drupe from many other fleshy fruits.

real_photo.label: Peach drupe showing fleshy tissue and hard stone
real_photo.alt: Real cross-section photograph of a peach showing the fleshy mesocarp and hard stone surrounding the seed
real_photo.focus: The peach flesh surrounds a hard inner stone. That hardened endocarp around the seed is the defining drupe feature.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY 2.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

gymnosperm.plain: A seed plant whose ovules and seeds are not enclosed inside an ovary.
gymnosperm.formal: A vascular seed plant bearing exposed ovules rather than angiosperm carpels.
gymnosperm.where: Think conifers, cycads, ginkgo and relatives.
gymnosperm.why: Explains why junipers make cones, not flowers and fruits.

scale-leaf.plain: A scale leaf is a tiny reduced leaf pressed closely against the twig like an overlapping roof shingle.
scale-leaf.formal: A reduced foliar organ that is short, appressed and scale-like.
scale-leaf.where: Inspect an adult juniper branchlet very closely. Follow the twig surface and look for many small overlapping leaf tips rather than broad flat blades.
scale-leaf.why: Scale-like adult foliage is a fast recognition feature in many Cupressaceae, including eastern redcedar.

real_photo.label: Scale-like adult foliage of Juniperus virginiana
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of Juniperus virginiana branchlets showing small scale-like leaves pressed against the stems
real_photo.focus: Each tiny overlapping green unit pressed against the twig is a scale leaf.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

seed-cone.plain: A seed cone is the conifer reproductive structure that bears ovules and later seeds. In junipers it becomes fleshy and berry-like.
seed-cone.formal: A strobilus bearing ovuliferous scale complexes and exposed ovules.
seed-cone.where: On junipers, look for the larger round green, blue or bluish structures on female plants rather than the much smaller pollen cones.
seed-cone.why: Knowing that a juniper 'berry' is really a modified seed cone prevents one of the most common conifer terminology mistakes.

real_photo.label: Juniper seed cones — fleshy, berry-like cones
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Juniperus communis showing fleshy seed cones
real_photo.focus: The round berry-like structures are seed cones. Their cone scales have become fleshy and fused-looking.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons photograph.

pollen-cone.plain: A pollen cone is a small conifer cone that produces and releases pollen.
pollen-cone.formal: A microsporangiate strobilus bearing pollen-producing microsporophylls.
pollen-cone.where: Look closely at seasonal branch tips and axils for small yellowish or tan cones that are much smaller than seed cones.
pollen-cone.why: Separating pollen cones from seed cones makes conifer reproduction much easier to understand.

real_photo.label: Juniper pollen cones
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of Juniperus communis branchlets bearing small pollen cones
real_photo.focus: The small clustered yellowish-tan structures are pollen cones. They produce pollen and do not develop into the fleshy seed cones.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

glaucous.plain: Glaucous describes a pale bluish-gray or whitish surface caused by a waxy bloom.
glaucous.formal: Bearing an epicuticular wax bloom that gives a pale or bluish appearance.
glaucous.where: Look for a dull blue-white coating on leaves, stems, or fruit; it often looks powdery or waxed rather than simply pale green.
glaucous.why: Glaucous bloom can be a strong field character on foliage and fruits.

real_photo.label: Glaucous waxy bloom on leaves
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of Eucalyptus tetragona leaves showing a pale glaucous waxy coating
real_photo.focus: The pale bluish-white cast on the leaf surface is the glaucous bloom.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain Wikimedia Commons photograph.

inferior-ovary.plain: An inferior ovary sits below the point where the sepals, petals and stamens attach.
inferior-ovary.formal: An ovary embedded below the insertion of other floral whorls.
inferior-ovary.where: Use a flower side view or section. Find the swollen ovary below the visible flower parts.
inferior-ovary.why: Inferior ovaries are a major family-level clue in groups such as Onagraceae and Rosaceae.

real_photo.label: Real flower section showing an inferior ovary
real_photo.alt: Real longitudinal section of a Pyrus communis flower showing the inferior ovary below the other floral parts
real_photo.focus: The ovary occupies the lower swollen portion of the flower. The other floral parts arise above it.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

hypanthium.plain: A hypanthium is a cup or tube of floral tissue around the ovary, formed from the bases of other flower parts.
hypanthium.formal: A floral structure formed by fused or extended basal portions of sepals, petals and/or stamens surrounding the gynoecium.
hypanthium.where: View the flower from the side or in section and look for a cup-like wall surrounding the ovary or fruits.
hypanthium.why: Hypanthium shape and how it relates to the ovary are important in groups such as Rosaceae and Onagraceae.

real_photo.label: Rose hypanthium opened to show the floral cup
real_photo.alt: Longitudinally opened Rosa pisocarpa structure showing the fleshy hypanthium wall around the internal fruits
real_photo.focus: Follow the fleshy outer cup surrounding the small internal fruits. That enclosing cup is the hypanthium.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

floral-tube.plain: A floral tube is the narrow tubular section below the expanded flower parts.
floral-tube.formal: A tubular floral structure formed by fused or elongated perianth/hypanthial tissues.
floral-tube.where: View an Oenothera-type flower from the side. Follow the petals downward and look for the narrow tube before you reach the ovary.
floral-tube.why: In Onagraceae, the floral tube and its relationship to the inferior ovary are useful family- and genus-level characters.

real_photo.label: Oenothera flower showing the narrow floral tube
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of Oenothera lindheimeri flowers showing the narrow floral tube below the expanded petals
real_photo.focus: Follow one flower from its petals toward the stem. The narrow section below the expanded flower is the floral tube.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain Wikimedia Commons photograph.

zygomorphic.plain: Zygomorphic means a flower has bilateral symmetry: only one main plane divides it into matching left and right halves.
zygomorphic.formal: Bilaterally symmetrical rather than radially symmetrical.
zygomorphic.where: Look straight at the flower and imagine folding it along different lines. If only one main line gives mirror-image halves, it is zygomorphic.
zygomorphic.why: Bilateral symmetry is a strong floral architecture clue and occurs in groups such as Lamiaceae and the former Gaura lineage within Oenothera.

real_photo.label: Zygomorphic Oenothera lindheimeri flower
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of Oenothera lindheimeri flowers showing bilateral rather than radial symmetry
real_photo.focus: Look at one open flower face-on. The petals and reproductive parts are arranged so one main plane produces left-right mirror halves.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same public-domain Oenothera image as the Floral tube lesson, with the overlay focused on symmetry.

exserted.plain: Exserted means a floral organ projects beyond the surrounding corolla or floral tube.
exserted.formal: Projecting beyond an enclosing organ, especially stamens or styles beyond the corolla.
exserted.where: Compare the tips of the stamens or style with the edge of the petals/corolla. If they extend clearly past it, they are exserted.
exserted.why: The degree of exsertion can be a conspicuous identification character in tubular and bilaterally symmetrical flowers.

real_photo.label: Oenothera lindheimeri with exserted stamens and style
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Oenothera lindheimeri flowers showing long stamens and style projecting beyond the petals
real_photo.focus: The stamens and style extend well beyond the main petal outline. That projection is exsertion.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

indehiscent.plain: A mature fruit that does not naturally open to release its seeds.
indehiscent.where: Inspect mature fruits and whether they open along valves or sutures.
indehiscent.why: Important for the hard few-seeded former-Gaura fruits.

accrescent.plain: Continuing to grow after flowering, often around or beneath the fruit.
accrescent.where: Compare the calyx at flowering and fruiting stages.
accrescent.why: Persimmon calyces can remain and enlarge beneath the berry.

berry.plain: A botanical berry is a fleshy fruit in which most of the fruit wall remains fleshy around the seeds.
berry.formal: A fleshy indehiscent fruit derived from one ovary, usually with seeds embedded in pulp.
berry.where: Look at a cross-section of a tomato, persimmon, grape or similar fruit. The seeds sit within fleshy ovary tissue rather than inside a hard stone.
berry.why: Botanical fruit terms do not match grocery-store categories; learning the internal structure prevents confusion between berries, drupes and aggregate fruits.

real_photo.label: Tomato cross-section — a true botanical berry
real_photo.alt: Real cross-section photograph of a tomato showing multiple seed-filled locules surrounded by fleshy fruit wall
real_photo.focus: The seeds are embedded within fleshy ovary tissue. There is no hard stone around a single seed, which is the basic berry pattern.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

dioecious.plain: Dioecious means male and female flowers are borne on separate individual plants.
dioecious.formal: A sexual system in which staminate and pistillate flowers are borne on different individuals.
dioecious.where: Compare multiple flowering individuals. One plant bears staminate flowers and a different plant bears pistillate flowers.
dioecious.why: This explains why a single female holly or juniper may not fruit if no compatible male plant is nearby.

real_photo.label: Male and female Sassafras flowers shown side by side
real_photo.alt: Real comparison photograph of male and female Sassafras flowers
real_photo.focus: The left flower is male/staminate and the right flower is female/pistillate. In a dioecious species these occur on separate plants.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 3.0 Wikimedia Commons comparison photograph.

samara.plain: A samara is a dry fruit with a wing that helps the seed-bearing fruit spin or glide away.
samara.where: Look at mature ash, elm or maple fruits and find the papery wing attached to the seed-bearing part.
samara.why: Wing shape and whether samaras occur singly or in pairs can be excellent family- and genus-level clues.

real_photo.label: Maple samara showing seed-bearing base and wing
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of a maple samara with a seed-bearing base and broad papery wing
real_photo.focus: The entire dry winged fruit is the samara. The papery portion is the wing; the thicker base contains the seed.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

apetalous.plain: Apetalous means a flower has no petals.
apetalous.where: Inspect the flower closely. Confirm that petals are truly absent rather than simply fallen or hidden.
apetalous.why: Some families and genera include flowers with no petals at all, so petal absence can be a useful structural clue.

real_photo.label: Apetalous flower — floral organs present but no petals
real_photo.alt: Public-domain botanical illustration of an apetalous Chenopodium flower with a calyx and stamens but no petals
real_photo.focus: The flower has a perianth/calyx and stamens, but there is no petal whorl between them.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain botanical illustration.

pome.plain: A pome is a fleshy Rosaceae fruit in which fleshy floral tissue surrounds the true ovary core.
pome.formal: An accessory fruit in which the hypanthium/receptacular tissue becomes fleshy around an inferior compound ovary.
pome.where: Look at a cross-section of an apple, pear, crabapple or hawthorn. Find the central core first, then compare it with the fleshy tissue outside it.
pome.why: The pome is a major Rosaceae fruit architecture and connects directly to the family’s hypanthium/inferior-ovary anatomy.

real_photo.label: Pome cross-section showing fleshy outer tissue and core
real_photo.alt: Real cross-section photograph of Pyrus pyrifolia showing the fleshy outer portion and central core of a pome
real_photo.focus: The central multi-carpellate core is the true ovary-derived fruit region. Much of the fleshy tissue outside it comes from surrounding floral tissue.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

drupelet.plain: A drupelet is one tiny drupe within an aggregate fruit such as a blackberry.
drupelet.formal: A small drupe derived from one carpel within an aggregate fruit.
drupelet.where: Look at one bead-like unit on a blackberry or raspberry rather than the entire fruit.
drupelet.why: Thinking in drupelets explains why a blackberry is not one botanical berry: it is many tiny drupes produced by one flower.

real_photo.label: One drupelet within a blackberry aggregate fruit
real_photo.alt: Real macro photograph of blackberries showing individual bead-like drupelets
real_photo.focus: Pick one glossy bead. That single unit is a drupelet; all the drupelets together make the aggregate fruit.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same CC BY-SA 3.0 blackberry photograph as the Aggregate fruit lesson, with the overlay focused on one component.

aggregate-fruit.plain: An aggregate fruit forms when one flower has several separate carpels and each carpel develops into its own small fruit unit.
aggregate-fruit.formal: A fruiting structure formed from multiple free carpels of a single flower.
aggregate-fruit.where: Look at a blackberry or raspberry. The whole structure came from one flower, but it is built from many small fruit units packed together.
aggregate-fruit.why: Aggregate fruit tells you about the flower’s multiple free carpels and helps separate fruit types that look superficially like simple berries.

real_photo.label: Blackberry aggregate fruit made of many drupelets
real_photo.alt: Real macro photograph of blackberries showing many bead-like drupelets forming one aggregate fruit
real_photo.focus: The entire blackberry is one aggregate fruit from one flower. Each bead-like unit is a separate drupelet.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 3.0 source photograph; the underlying Wikimedia Commons image is unmodified.

floral-disk.plain: A floral disk is a ring or pad of tissue around the flower’s reproductive organs, often producing nectar.
floral-disk.formal: A disk-shaped floral structure associated with the reproductive organs, commonly nectariferous.
floral-disk.where: Look in the center of the flower around or just below the stamens and ovary. The disk may be a raised ring, cushion, or lobed pad.
floral-disk.why: A floral disk is a useful supporting character in families such as Sapindaceae and Anacardiaceae.

real_photo.label: Top view of a floral disk surrounding the flower center
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of a Causonis tenuifolia flower showing the yellow floral disk from above
real_photo.focus: The raised yellow ring/pad surrounding the reproductive center is the floral disk.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons photograph; the source image specifically documents the floral disc.

pyrene.plain: A pyrene is one hard, seed-containing stone inside a drupaceous fruit.
pyrene.formal: A hardened endocarp unit enclosing one or more seeds within a drupaceous fruit.
pyrene.where: Open or dissect a suitable ripe fruit when appropriate and separate the hard internal units from the surrounding flesh.
pyrene.why: Ilex fruits contain multiple pyrenes, so learning this term helps distinguish the hard internal stones from the whole fleshy fruit.

real_photo.label: Two pyrenes removed from a fleshy fruit
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of two Pyracantha pyrenes removed from a fruit
real_photo.focus: Each hard internal unit is one pyrene. The pyrene is the hardened fruit-wall structure surrounding a seed.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

staminode.plain: A staminode is a sterile or reduced stamen that does not produce functional pollen.
staminode.where: In a pistillate or specialized flower, compare the small stamen-like structures with normal pollen-bearing stamens.
staminode.why: Staminodes help explain how flowers can retain the shape of a stamen even after losing its pollen-producing function.

real_photo.label: Scientific illustration showing a staminode in a pistillate flower
real_photo.alt: Scientific botanical illustration of Matayba ayangannensis including a pistillate flower and labeled staminode detail
real_photo.focus: Use the pistillate-flower detail marked G in the source plate. The reduced stamen-like structure is the staminode.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a CC BY 4.0 scientific illustration from PhytoKeys.

pistillode.plain: A pistillode is a reduced, nonfunctional pistil left in a flower that functions as male.
pistillode.where: Look in the center of a staminate flower. If a small sterile gynoecium remains among the functional stamens, it is a pistillode.
pistillode.why: Pistillodes are useful when comparing male and female flowers in dioecious or otherwise unisexual species.

real_photo.label: Scientific illustration showing a pistillode in a staminate flower
real_photo.credit: Pedro Acevedo-Rodríguez · CC BY 4.0 / CC BY 3.0
real_photo.alt: Scientific botanical illustration of Allophylastrum frutescens including a staminate flower, nectary disc, stamens and pistillode
real_photo.focus: Use the staminate-flower detail and the separate pistillode drawing in the source plate. The reduced central gynoecium is the pistillode.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the PhytoKeys scientific illustration; the source explicitly labels the pistillode.

coriaceous.plain: Coriaceous means thick, firm, and leathery in texture.
coriaceous.formal: Having the texture or consistency of leather.
coriaceous.where: Observe a mature leaf’s thickness, stiffness, and durable surface rather than judging color alone.
coriaceous.why: Leathery versus thin or papery foliage is a useful vegetative character in many woody plants.

real_photo.label: Thick coriaceous Diospyros leaves
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Diospyros maritima showing thick leathery coriaceous leaves
real_photo.focus: The blades are thick and firm rather than thin and papery. That leathery consistency is coriaceous.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons image specifically titled for coriaceous leaves.

distichous.plain: Leaves arranged in two rows along opposite sides of a twig.
distichous.formal: Arranged in two ranks in a single plane.
distichous.where: Look down the length of a leafy twig.
distichous.why: Common in elms and useful for whole-twig architecture.

oblique-base.plain: One side of the leaf base extends lower than the other.
oblique-base.formal: A leaf base whose two sides are unequal or offset.
oblique-base.where: Look where the blade meets the petiole.

serrate.plain: Serrate means the leaf edge has sharp saw-like teeth pointing generally toward the tip.
serrate.formal: Bearing sharp marginal teeth directed toward the leaf apex.
serrate.where: Look closely along the blade margin and follow the direction of the tooth tips.
serrate.why: Margin type is a common key character and helps separate similar trees, shrubs, and herbs.

real_photo.label: Serrate leaf margin
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of a Lantana camara leaf showing a serrate margin
real_photo.focus: Each sharp tooth along the edge points generally toward the leaf tip, producing the serrate saw-like margin.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

racemose.plain: An inflorescence whose main axis keeps growing while flowers open from older to younger positions.
racemose.formal: An indeterminate inflorescence architecture with continued apical growth.
racemose.where: Look along a spike, raceme, or head and note flowering sequence.
racemose.why: Modern Verbenaceae commonly uses racemose/spicate/head architectures.

real_photo.label: Real flowering raceme
real_photo.alt: Photograph of a flowering Maianthemum stellatum raceme
real_photo.focus: Trace the single main axis. Individual stalked flowers arise along that unbranched axis — the basic raceme pattern.

terminal-style.plain: A style arising from the top of the ovary rather than from between deep ovary lobes.
terminal-style.formal: A style inserted apically on the ovary.
terminal-style.where: Inspect the gynoecium after moving the corolla aside.
terminal-style.why: A useful local distinction from the common gynobasic Lamiaceae pattern.

didynamous.plain: Four stamens arranged as two longer and two shorter.
didynamous.formal: An androecium of four stamens in two unequal pairs.
didynamous.where: Look inside a tubular bilabiate flower.
didynamous.why: Common in Verbenaceae and Lamiaceae, so it supports but does not alone separate them.

winged-seed.plain: A seed with a papery wing that helps it travel on air.
winged-seed.formal: A seed bearing flattened membranous extensions that increase dispersal area.
winged-seed.where: Open a mature dry capsule or inspect naturally released seeds.
winged-seed.why: Flat winged seeds are a high-value Bignoniaceae clue.

stylopodium.plain: A swollen pad at the top of an Apiaceae ovary where the styles arise.
stylopodium.formal: An expanded conical or disk-like base of the styles, often nectariferous, atop the ovary in Apiaceae.
stylopodium.where: Use a hand lens on a flower or young fruit.
stylopodium.why: A technical but useful Apiaceae confirmation.

interpetiolar-stipule.plain: A stipule positioned between the petioles of an opposite leaf pair.
interpetiolar-stipule.formal: A stipular structure occupying the node between opposite petiole bases.
interpetiolar-stipule.where: Look directly between opposite leaves at a node.
interpetiolar-stipule.why: One of the strongest vegetative Rubiaceae clues.

hilum.plain: The hilum is the scar on a seed marking where it was attached inside the fruit.
hilum.formal: The attachment scar marking the former connection between seed and funiculus/placenta.
hilum.where: Inspect a clean mature seed and look for an oval, linear, or differently colored scar on the seed coat.
hilum.why: Hilum size, position, and shape can be diagnostic in several plant groups.

real_photo.label: Seed diagram showing the hilum
real_photo.alt: Botanical diagram comparing monocot and dicot seeds with the hilum labeled on the dicot seed
real_photo.focus: On the dicot seed, the hilum marks the former point of attachment to the fruit.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons seed anatomy diagram that explicitly labels the hilum.

parallel-veined.plain: Parallel-veined leaves have major veins running side by side from near the base toward the tip.
parallel-veined.formal: Venation in which primary veins course approximately parallel through the blade.
parallel-veined.where: Hold the leaf flat or to the light and trace several major veins at once.
parallel-veined.why: Parallel venation strongly supports monocot identification when combined with other characters.

real_photo.label: Real leaf with parallel venation
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a leaf showing major veins running approximately parallel through the blade
real_photo.focus: Trace several veins from the lower blade upward. They run alongside one another rather than forming a branching net.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

loculicidal.plain: A capsule that splits open through the middle of each chamber.
loculicidal.formal: Dehiscence along the dorsal suture or midline of each locule.
loculicidal.why: A common technical capsule character in Commelinaceae and other families.

anther-valve.plain: A flap of anther wall that lifts open to release pollen.
anther-valve.formal: A valvular mode of anther dehiscence in which portions of the anther wall open as hinged flaps.
anther-valve.where: Use magnification on a mature Berberis anther.
anther-valve.why: Valve-opening anthers are a memorable Berberis character.

nectary.formal: A secretory organ or tissue producing nectar.
nectary.where: Look near the base of petals, stamens, or floral disks depending on the plant.
nectary.why: Nectary position can be a useful floral character.

hemiparasite.plain: A green plant that photosynthesizes but also taps another plant for water and nutrients.
hemiparasite.formal: A photosynthetic parasite obtaining water and/or solutes from a host through haustoria.
hemiparasite.where: The host connection is usually below ground in local Orobanchaceae.
hemiparasite.why: Explains why many Orobanchaceae look fully green despite being parasitic.

haustorium.plain: A specialized organ a parasitic plant uses to connect to host tissue.
haustorium.formal: A penetrative absorptive organ forming a physiological connection between parasite and host.
haustorium.where: Usually at roots or stems depending on the parasite; do not uproot plants just to see it.
haustorium.why: It is the defining biological connection in parasitic plant families.

bract.plain: A bract is a modified leaf associated with a flower or flower cluster.
bract.formal: A foliar organ subtending a flower, branch, or inflorescence.
bract.where: Look directly beneath a flower or along the flowering axis for a leaf-like structure that is part of the reproductive display.
bract.why: Bracts can be more conspicuous than the true flowers, so learning to separate them prevents major ID mistakes.

real_photo.label: Bracts surrounding much smaller true flowers
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of Bougainvillea showing large purple bracts surrounding tiny white true flowers
real_photo.focus: The large purple structures are bracts. The tiny white structures nestled among them are the true flowers.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

tendril.plain: A tendril is a slender coiling organ that wraps around nearby support and helps a vine climb.
tendril.formal: A modified stem, leaf, leaflet, or inflorescence specialized for climbing.
tendril.where: Inspect a vine node and follow the tendril back to its exact point of origin; that origin can help identify the plant group.
tendril.why: Tendril placement and structure can separate vines such as Passiflora, Vitis and Parthenocissus.

real_photo.label: Coiling Passiflora tendril
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a Passiflora edulis tendril coiling around support
real_photo.focus: The thin curling structure is the tendril. It coils around support rather than functioning as a normal leaf blade.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

androgynophore.plain: A stalk that lifts both the stamens and ovary above the rest of the flower.
androgynophore.formal: An elongate floral axis bearing both androecium and gynoecium above the perianth.
androgynophore.where: Look at the center of a passionflower above the corona.

aril.plain: A fleshy or specialized covering that grows around part or all of a seed.
aril.formal: An accessory seed covering arising from the funiculus or seed attachment region.

leaf-opposed.plain: Positioned directly across the stem from a leaf rather than in its axil.
leaf-opposed.formal: Inserted on the node opposite a leaf.
leaf-opposed.where: Check grape-vine nodes for tendrils or inflorescences opposite leaves.

calyptra.plain: A cap-like structure that comes off as one piece.
calyptra.formal: A cap or hood formed by coherent floral parts; in Vitis the petals may detach together as a calyptra.
calyptra.where: Watch or inspect opening grape flowers.

triplinerved.plain: A leaf with three strong primary veins arising from or near its base.
triplinerved.formal: Bearing three prominent primary veins originating basally or subbasally.
triplinerved.where: Hold a Celtis leaf flat and trace veins from the petiole.

cystolith.plain: A mineral deposit inside certain plant cells that can contribute to a rough leaf texture.
cystolith.formal: A mineralized intracellular body, commonly calcium carbonate, associated with specialized epidermal cells.
cystolith.where: Usually microscopic, though associated roughness may be felt or seen.

retinaculum.plain: A hook-like structure inside some capsules that supports the seed.
retinaculum.formal: A modified funicular or placental structure associated with seed support and release in Acanthaceae.
retinaculum.where: Open a mature Acanthaceae capsule and inspect beneath the seeds.
retinaculum.why: One of the strongest family-level characters for Acanthaceae.

perianth.plain: The non-reproductive outer flower parts taken together.
perianth.formal: The collective calyx and corolla, or equivalent undifferentiated floral envelope.
perianth.where: Look outside the stamens and pistil.
perianth.why: Useful when sepals and petals are unusual or not cleanly separated.

gynostemium.plain: A compact reproductive column where stamens and style-related tissues are closely united.
gynostemium.formal: A columnar floral structure formed by union or close association of androecial and gynoecial tissues.
gynostemium.where: Look inside an Aristolochia flower tube.
gynostemium.why: A key part of Aristolochia reproductive architecture.

areole.plain: An areole is the specialized cactus growth point that produces spines, hairs, branches, or flowers.
areole.formal: A highly specialized axillary bud/short-shoot structure diagnostic of Cactaceae.
areole.where: Look for repeated small cushions or pads on the cactus stem or cladode.
areole.why: Areoles are the defining structural feature of Cactaceae.

real_photo.label: Cactus areoles in close-up
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of cactus areoles with spine clusters emerging from specialized cushion-like points
real_photo.focus: Each small cushion-like point from which the spines emerge is one areole.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons close-up of cactus areoles.

glochid.plain: A glochid is a tiny barbed bristle produced in Opuntioideae areoles.
glochid.formal: A minute, readily detached, barbed spine characteristic of Opuntioideae.
glochid.where: Look closely at prickly-pear areoles without touching them. Glochids often form dense fuzzy-looking tufts among or around larger spines.
glochid.why: Glochids are a strong structural clue for prickly pears and their close relatives.

real_photo.label: Opuntia glochids at 20× magnification
real_photo.alt: Magnified real photograph of Opuntia areoles showing dense clusters of tiny barbed glochids and larger spines
real_photo.focus: The dense short golden-brown bristles are glochids. The much larger rigid structures are ordinary spines.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons macro explicitly documented as Opuntia glochids at 20× magnification.

cladode.plain: A flattened or modified stem doing the photosynthetic job people often mistake for a leaf.
cladode.formal: A modified photosynthetic stem or branch resembling a leaf.
cladode.where: In Opuntia, the flat pad itself is a stem segment.

succulent.plain: Thick fleshy tissue adapted to store water.
succulent.formal: Water-storing vegetative tissue with enlarged parenchymatous organs.
succulent.where: Look at stems or leaves for fleshy water-storage structure.
succulent.why: Useful ecology/morphology, but not enough by itself to identify Cactaceae.

urceolate.plain: Shaped like a little urn: swollen below and narrower at the opening.
urceolate.formal: A sympetalous corolla shape resembling an urn or pitcher.
urceolate.where: View an Ericaceae flower from the side.
urceolate.why: Common in many Ericaceae flowers such as Arbutus and Vaccinium.

poricidal.plain: Releasing pollen through small pores instead of long slits.
poricidal.formal: Dehiscing through terminal or subterminal pores.

husk.plain: An outer covering around a nut or seed-bearing structure.
husk.formal: A fleshy, fibrous, or leathery outer fruit/perianth-derived layer surrounding a nut.
husk.where: Look around a walnut before the hard shell is exposed.
husk.why: A husked nut is a strong Juglandaceae fruit cue.

chambered-pith.plain: Stem pith divided into a series of little internal chambers.
chambered-pith.formal: Pith interrupted by transverse partitions or diaphragms.
chambered-pith.where: Visible in a clean twig cross/longitudinal section when appropriate.
chambered-pith.why: A useful secondary Juglans twig character.

annular-stipule-scar.plain: A ring-like scar left around the twig by a stipule.
annular-stipule-scar.formal: An encircling nodal scar produced by a sheathing stipule.
annular-stipule-scar.where: Inspect a sycamore twig at a node after leaf/stipule fall.

aliases: male and female flowers on one plant
monoecious.plain: Monoecious means one individual plant bears separate male and female flowers.
monoecious.formal: A sexual system in which staminate and pistillate flowers occur on the same individual.
monoecious.where: Inspect one flowering plant and look for two distinct flower types on that same individual.
monoecious.why: Monoecious plants separate male and female functions into different flowers without separating them onto different plants.

real_photo.label: Male and female flowers on the same Comptonia plant
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Comptonia peregrina showing a male catkin above and a female flower below on the same plant
real_photo.focus: The catkin above is male and the red structure below is female. Both occur on the same individual plant.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 3.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph; the source description identifies both flower sexes.

stipe.plain: The stalk of a fern frond below the leafy blade.
stipe.formal: The petiole-like basal stalk of a fern frond.
stipe.where: Follow the frond from the rhizome up to the first blade divisions.
stipe.why: Basic vocabulary for reading fern architecture.

pinna.plain: A pinna is one primary division of a pinnate fern frond.
pinna.formal: A primary segment of a pinnate fern blade.
pinna.where: Look at the fern’s main rachis and identify the large repeated side divisions attached directly to it.
pinna.why: Once you can separate the whole frond from individual pinnae, fern descriptions become much easier to follow.

real_photo.label: Pinnate fern frond showing individual pinnae
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a pinnate fern frond with repeated pinnae along the main rachis
real_photo.focus: Each large side division attached directly to the main rachis is one pinna.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a GFDL Wikimedia Commons fern photograph.

pinnule.plain: A pinnule is a smaller secondary division within a pinna.
pinnule.formal: A secondary division of a pinnate fern frond.
pinnule.where: First identify a pinna, then look within it for the next repeated level of subdivision.
pinnule.why: Pinna versus pinnule is essential terminology when comparing more finely divided ferns.

real_photo.label: Fern pinnule with sori on its underside
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of a Dryopteris dilatata pinnule showing sori on the underside
real_photo.focus: The entire small divided blade shown here is one pinnule. The brown reproductive clusters on it are sori.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

sorus.plain: A sorus is a cluster of many spore-producing sporangia on a fern.
sorus.formal: An aggregation of sporangia on a fern frond.
sorus.where: Usually turn a fertile frond over. Look for repeated dots, lines or marginal patches on the underside.
sorus.why: Sorus shape and position are among the most important fern-identification characters.

real_photo.label: Round sori on the underside of a fern frond
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of the underside of Polypodium vulgare showing many round sori
real_photo.focus: Each brown round cluster is one sorus. Each sorus contains many much smaller sporangia.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons photograph.

sporangium.plain: A sporangium is one tiny capsule-like organ that produces and releases spores.
sporangium.where: Use magnification. A sorus is made of many individual sporangia packed together.
sporangium.why: Understanding sporangium versus sorus is the fern equivalent of understanding one floret versus a whole flower head.

real_photo.label: Fern sporangia under scanning electron microscopy
real_photo.alt: Scanning electron micrograph of fern sporangia in different stages of spore release
real_photo.focus: Each capsule-like body is one sporangium. Multiple sporangia are grouped together into a sorus on the fern.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 3.0 scanning electron micrograph.

false-indusium.plain: A false indusium is the rolled or folded edge of a fern blade that bends over and protects the sori.
false-indusium.formal: A recurved or modified laminar margin sheltering marginal sori, rather than a separate true indusial membrane.
false-indusium.where: Inspect the margin of a fertile maidenhair or cliffbrake-type fern from below. Look for the leaf edge itself folding over the reproductive structures.
false-indusium.why: This differs from a true indusium because the protective flap is made from the leaf margin rather than a separate membrane.

real_photo.label: Adiantum false indusium formed by the folded leaf margin
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of an Adiantum false indusium where the leaf margin folds over the sori
real_photo.focus: The protective flap is actually the rolled leaf margin. That folded edge is the false indusium.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

heterophylly.plain: One plant makes noticeably different leaf forms under different conditions.
heterophylly.formal: Production of morphologically distinct leaf types on the same individual, often in response to environment or developmental stage.
heterophylly.where: Compare submerged and emergent leaves on the same aquatic plant.
heterophylly.why: Aquatic plants can look like different species above and below water.

phyllode.plain: A flattened leaf-like structure that functions like a blade even when the usual blade is reduced.
phyllode.formal: A flattened photosynthetic petiole or modified leaf axis functioning in place of a conventional lamina.
phyllode.where: In the local Sagittaria lesson, inspect the narrow submerged leaf-like structures.
phyllode.why: It explains why submerged Sagittaria can look unlike the emergent plant.

enantiostyly.plain: Flowers occur in left- and right-handed forms because the style and stamens switch sides.
enantiostyly.formal: A floral polymorphism in which reproductive organs are reciprocally deflected to opposite sides in different flowers.
enantiostyly.why: It is a memorable reproductive morphology lesson and pollination adaptation.

salverform.plain: A flower with a long narrow tube that suddenly opens into a flat face.
salverform.formal: A sympetalous corolla with an elongated narrow tube and abruptly spreading limb.
salverform.where: View the flower from the side.
salverform.why: Corolla shape is a useful descriptive and comparative character.

staminate.plain: A staminate flower functions as male: it has functional stamens and no functional pistil.
staminate.formal: A unisexual flower bearing functional stamens and lacking a functional gynoecium.
staminate.where: Look for pollen-bearing anthers and compare the center with a pistillate flower of the same species.
staminate.why: Recognizing staminate flowers helps you read unisexual plants and understand male-versus-female reproductive roles.

real_photo.label: Staminate Sassafras flower
real_photo.alt: Real comparison photograph showing a male Sassafras flower with multiple stamens
real_photo.focus: Use the flower on the left. Its conspicuous stamens and anthers make it staminate.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same CC BY-SA 3.0 Sassafras comparison photo as the Dioecious lesson, focused on the male flower.

pistillate.plain: A pistillate flower functions as female: it has a functional pistil and no functional stamens.
pistillate.formal: A unisexual flower bearing a functional gynoecium and lacking functional stamens.
pistillate.where: Look for the central stigma/style/ovary structure and compare it with a staminate flower of the same species.
pistillate.why: Pistillate flowers develop the fruit after successful pollination.

real_photo.label: Pistillate Sassafras flower
real_photo.alt: Real comparison photograph showing a female Sassafras flower with a central pistil
real_photo.focus: Use the flower on the right. Its central pistil is the functional female reproductive structure.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same CC BY-SA 3.0 Sassafras comparison photo as the Dioecious lesson, focused on the female flower.

pollinarium.plain: The whole milkweed pollen-transfer unit, usually two pollinia linked by connecting arms to a small central clip.
pollinarium.formal: A pollen-transfer complex consisting of pollinia connected by translator arms to a corpusculum.
pollinarium.where: Look at the tiny removable pollen apparatus associated with the stigmatic slits of a milkweed gynostegium.
pollinarium.why: It explains how milkweed pollen is removed and transferred as a single mechanical unit rather than loose grains.

real_photo.label: Real Asclepias asperula pollinarium
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of Asclepias asperula pollinarium
real_photo.focus: Look for the two pollen masses joined through the central transport apparatus.

corpusculum.plain: The tiny central clip-like part of a milkweed pollinarium that catches on a pollinator.
corpusculum.formal: The central hardened body of the pollinarium that connects translator arms leading to the pollinia.
corpusculum.where: Look at the center of a detached milkweed pollinarium between the two pollen masses.
corpusculum.why: It is the mechanical attachment point that helps a pollinator pull the pollinarium from the flower.

real_photo.label: Pollinarium showing the central corpusculum
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of a milkweed pollinarium
real_photo.focus: The corpusculum is the small central connector between the arms leading to the two pollinia.

raceme.plain: A raceme is an unbranched flower cluster with individual flowers on short stalks along one main axis.
raceme.formal: An indeterminate, unbranched inflorescence bearing pedicellate flowers along an elongated main axis.
raceme.where: Trace the flower cluster from bottom to top and look for one main axis with separate flower stalks coming off its sides.
raceme.why: Recognizing a raceme helps separate one common inflorescence architecture from spikes, panicles, umbels and heads.

real_photo.label: Real raceme with one main axis and stalked flowers
real_photo.alt: Photograph of Maianthemum stellatum showing a raceme of stalked white flowers
real_photo.focus: Follow the central axis. Each flower attaches by its own small stalk, called a pedicel.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.
